text: OLIGOMORPHIC GROUPS AND TENSOR CATEGORIES
NATE HARMAN AND ANDREW SNOWDEN

Abstract. Given an oligomorphic group $G$ and a measure $\mu$ for $G$ (in a sense that we introduce), we define a rigid tensor category $\underline { { \mathrm { P e r m } } } ( G ; \mu )$ of “permutation modules,” and, in certain cases, an abelian envelope $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ; \mu )$ of this category. When $G$ is the infinite symmetric group, this recovers Deligne’s interpolation category. Other choices for $G$ lead to fundamentally new tensor categories. For example, we construct the first known semisimple pre-Tannakian categories in positive characteristic with super-exponential growth. One interesting aspect of our construction is that, unlike previous work in this direction, our categories are concrete: the objects are modules over a ring, and the tensor product receives a universal bi-linear map. Central to our constructions is a novel theory of integration on oligomorphic groups, which could be of more general interest. Classifying the measures on an oligomorphic group appears to be a difficult problem, which we solve in only a few cases.

1. Introduction

1.1. Overview. The collection of all finite dimensional representations of an algebraic group is an abelian category that comes equipped with a symmetric tensor product. By abstracting the essential properties of this example, one arrives at the notion of a pre-Tannakian category (see Definition 13.1). These categories have received much attention in the literature, yet, despite this, the general landscape of pre-Tannakian categories is still essentially unknown. In this paper, we take a step towards understanding these objects better.

We begin by recalling some relevant previous work. Deligne [Del3], building on earlier work [Del1, DM], observed that one can construct new examples pre-Tannakian categories by “interpolating” known families. By interpolating the categories $\mathrm { R e p } ( \mathfrak { S } _ { n } )$ for $n \in \mathbf N$ , he constructed a new pre-Tannakian category $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ^ { \mathrm { a b } } ( \mathfrak { S } _ { t } )$ for $t \in \mathbf { C }$ . Deligne’s work has generated intense interest, and there has been a slew of ensuing papers, such as [CO2, CO1, Eti1, Eti2, EAH, EAHS, Har, Har2, Mei]. In particular, Knop [Kno1, Kno2] put Deligne’s method into a general framework, and used his theory to construct other examples, such as interpolation categories for finite linear groups.

Currently, the biggest roadblock to understanding general pre-Tannakian categories is the paucity of specimens: the only known examples are the classical representation categories of algebraic (super)groups, and categories obtained from them by interpolation (at least in characteristic zero1). It is hard to extrapolate from these examples what a general pre-Tannakian category might look like.

The purpose of this paper is develop a new kind of representation theory for a class of groups, called oligomorphic groups, which leads to many new examples of pre-Tannakian tensor categories. To be a bit more precise, we introduce a notion of measure for an oligomorphic group. Given a measure $\mu$ for $G$ , we define a non-abelian tensor category Perm $( G ; \mu )$ of “permutation modules.” In certain cases, we also construct a (locally) pre-Tannakian category $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ; \mu )$ .
Before describing the details of this construction, we wish to highlight what we see as the main accomplishments of this paper.

list_items: (a) New examples. We construct pre-Tannakian categories that are fundamentally different than previously known examples. For example, we construct a pre-Tannakian category associated to the oligomorphic group $\mathrm { A u t } ( \mathbf { R } , < )$ . This category is semisimple in all characteristics, and is the first example of a semi-simple category in positive characteristic of super-exponential growth. We prove that this category cannot be obtained by interpolating known categories. Further work on this category (discussed in §1.7.3) has revealed many other interesting properties.

(b) Concrete nature. In contrast to all previous work in this area, our categories are concrete. In other words, we do not simply formally construct a pre-Tannakian category, but we define a new class of representations that happens to form such a category. These representations have their own internal structure, which can be very useful when studying them; for example, we describe the tensor product of representations via a universal property. This concrete interpretation is new even for the previously known examples, such as Deligne’s category.

1In positive characteristic, there are some very different examples, such as the Verlinde category. These examples run orthogonal to this paper, so we do not discuss them further.

(c) Abelian envelopes. To construct $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ^ { \mathrm { a b } } ( \mathfrak { S } _ { t } )$ , Deligne first constructed a non-abelian category $\mathrm { R e p } ( \mathfrak { S } _ { t } )$ by diagrammatics, and then produced an abelian envelope. This is typical of the subject: it is often easier to construct a preliminary non-abelian category, and then one is left with the problem of finding an abelian envelope. In the work of Deligne and Knop, the construction of the abelian envelope ultimately relies on the fact that certain endomorphism rings are semi-simple, which is proven by explicitly identifying them with group algebras.

We give a new method for attacking this problem that does not require explicitly identifying the rings. Our method recovers results of Comes–Ostrik [CO2] on Deligne’s category, and applies to Knop’s category in cases where previous methods do not. Our method seems necessary for handling the new examples we construct. See §1.5.2 for more details.
(d) Theory of integration. We develop a new theory of measures and integration for oligomorphic groups. This could very well be of interest beyond our applications to tensor categories.

There is one additional important remark to make here. The pre-Tannakian categories we produce using oligomorphic groups are not simply a curious class of examples: in followup work [HS4], we show that they account for all “discrete” pre-Tannakian categories (see §1.7.1). We thus see our theory as a step towards classification of pre-Tannakian categories.

In the remainder of the introduction, we explain our constructions and results in more detail, and attempt to motivate them. We also discuss connections to previous work, and some important problems coming out of our work.

1.2. Motivation. The symmetric group ${ \mathfrak { S } } _ { n }$ acts on the set $\Omega _ { n } = \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ . Linearizing this action, one obtains the permutation representation $X _ { n }$ of ${ \mathfrak { S } } _ { n }$ . In the Deligne category $\mathrm { R e p } ( \mathfrak { S } _ { t } )$ , there is an analogous object $X$ . The defining feature of Deligne’s category is that small tensor powers of $X$ behave like small tensor powers of $X _ { n }$ when $n$ is large. The central ideas of this paper came from trying to understand how to make sense of this property in an elegant manner from the point of view of representation theory. There are really two problems to tackle.
The first problem is to understand mapping spaces. We have

$$
\operatorname {H o m} (X ^ {\otimes r}, X ^ {\otimes s}) = \lim  _ {n \to \infty} \operatorname {H o m} (X _ {n} ^ {\otimes r}, X _ {n} ^ {\otimes s})
$$

in the sense that the left side is the stable value of the right side. We would like to have a description of the stable value in terms of some concrete representation theoretic object. To this end, let $\mathfrak { S }$ be the infinite symmetric group, i.e., the group of all permutations of $\Omega = \{ 1 , 2 , \dots \}$ . Then $\mathrm { H o m } ( X _ { n } ^ { \otimes r } , X _ { n } ^ { \otimes s } )$ is the linearization of the set of ${ \mathfrak { S } } _ { n }$ -orbits on $\Omega _ { n } ^ { r + s }$ , and we have
in the same sense as the previous equation. Thus the mapping spaces in Deligne’s category can be described directly in terms of $\mathfrak { S }$ and its action on $\Omega$ .

The second problem is to understand the origin of the parameter $t$ in terms of the group $\mathfrak { S }$ . This parameter records the categorical dimension of the basic object $X$ . The analogous object $X _ { n }$ has dimension $n$ . This reflects the fact that $\Omega _ { n }$ has cardinality $n$ , or, equivalently, that the stabilizer ${ \mathfrak { S } } _ { n } ( 1 )$ of 1 has index $n$ in ${ \mathfrak { S } } _ { n }$ . It is thus sensible to say that the parameter $t$ is recording a formal notion of index for the subgroup ${ \mathfrak { S } } ( 1 )$ of $\mathfrak { S }$ . This led us to the
NATE HARMAN AND ANDREW SNOWDEN

notion of a generalized index (Definition 3.24): such is a rule assigning a number to each containment of open subgroups of $\mathfrak { S }$ , for which certain natural axioms hold. We prove that a complex-valued generalized index on $\mathfrak { S }$ is completely determined by the index of ${ \mathfrak { S } } ( 1 )$ , which can take any value. This provides a clear explanation, directly in terms of $\mathfrak { S }$ , for why Deligne’s category has a single parameter.

There is a reformulation of the notion of generalized index that will actually be more convenient for us. Instead of saying that $V \subset U$ has some index $a$ , we say that the quotient set $U / V$ has measure $a$ . For example, $\Omega$ itself has measure $t$ . We axiomatize this notion of measure in what follows, and show that measures are equivalent to generalized indices.

The above perspective on Deligne’s category lends itself very well to generalization, wherein the infinite symmetric group is replaced by a permutation group $( G , \Omega )$ . For this to work, two key properties must hold. First, $G$ must have finitely many orbits on $\Omega ^ { n }$ for each $n$ , to ensure that mapping spaces are finite dimensional; this is the oligomorphic property. And second, we must have a measure for $G$ . This paper carries out this procedure in detail, and studies the resulting tensor categories.

list_items: 1.3. The constructions. The main definitions and constructions in this paper come by simply following the preceding discussion to its logical ends. We now provide a summary.
1.3.1. Oligomorphic groups. We begin by introducing the first of two key definitions:

text: Definition 1.1 (Cameron). An oligomorphic group2 is a group $G$ with a given faithful action on a set $\Omega$ such that $G$ has finitely many orbits on $\Omega ^ { n }$ for all $n \geq 0$ . 

The most basic example of an oligomorphic group is the infinite symmetric group $\mathfrak { S }$ acting on the set $\Omega = \{ 1 , 2 , . . . \}$ . Some more examples are given in §1.4. We refer to Cameron’s excellent book [Cam3] for general background on the subject.

Fix an oligomorphic group $G$ . The group $G$ carries a natural topology, where the basic open subgroups are stabilizer groups on powers of $\Omega$ (see §2.2 for details). We say that an action of $G$ on a set $X$ is smooth if every stabilizer is open. Since we essentially only use smooth actions, we adopt the convention that “ $G$ -set” means “set with a smooth action of $G$ .” We say that a $G$ -set is finitary if it has finitely many orbits. Oligomorphic groups have the important property that a product of two finitary $G$ -sets is finitary.

Suppose that $X$ is a $G$ -set. We often need to work with subsets of $X$ that are stable under some open subgroup, which we would prefer not to name. We therefore introduce the following concept: a $\hat { G }$ -subset of $X$ is one stable under some open subgroup. We also define a notion of $\hat { G }$ -set without an ambient $G$ -set; see §2.5. A typical example is the fiber (over some point) of the map $\Omega ^ { [ 2 ] } \to \Omega$ encountered in §1.2. Figure 1 depicts some other examples of $\tilde { \mathcal { S } }$ -subsets. Intuitively, we think of $\hat { G }$ as an infinitesimal neighborhood of the identity in $G$ . The fact that every $G$ -set comes equipped with a canonical algebra of subsets (the $\hat { G }$ -subsets) is an important feature of oligomorphic groups.
1.3.2. Measures and integration. We now introduce the second key definition of this paper. Fix a commutative ring $k$ .
Definition 1.2. A measure for $G$ with values in $k$ is a rule $\mu$ that associates to each finitary $\hat { G }$ -set $X$ a value $\mu ( X ) \in k$ such that the following conditions hold:
(a) Isomorphism invariance: if $X$ and $Y$ are isomorphic then $\mu ( X ) = \mu ( Y )$

Example 1.3. Given $t \in \mathbf { C }$ , there is a unique $\mathbf { C }$ -valued measure $\mu _ { t }$ for the infinite symmetric group $\mathfrak { S }$ satisfying $\mu _ { t } ( \Omega ) = t$ . This measure also satisfies $\mu _ { t } ( \Omega ^ { \left[ 2 \right] } ) = t ( t - 1 )$ and $\mu _ { t } ( F ) = t - 1$ , where $F ^ { \prime }$ is any fiber of the map $\Omega ^ { [ 2 ] } \to \Omega$ . 

Constructing and classifying measures for oligomorphic groups seems to be a difficult problem. To this end, we introduce a ring $\Theta ( G )$ as follows: for each finitary $\hat { G }$ -set $X$ , there is a class $[ X ]$ , and these classes satisfy analogs of (a)–(e) above. The significance of this ring is that it receives a universal measure $\mu _ { \mathrm { u n i v } }$ , defined by $\mu _ { \mathrm { u n i v } } ( X ) = [ X ]$ . Thus giving a $k$ -valued measure on $G$ is equivalent to giving a ring homomorphism $\Theta ( G ) \to k$ . We set $\Theta ( G )$ aside for the time being, but will return to it later.

Suppose now that we happen to have a $k$ -valued measure $\mu$ . We then obtain a theory of integration, as follows. Let $X$ be a $\hat { G }$ -set. A Schwartz function on $X$ is a $k$ -valued function that is smooth (i.e., invariant under an open subgroup) and of finitary support. We let ${ \mathcal { C } } ( X )$ be the set of all such functions, which we term Schwartz space. Suppose $\varphi \in \mathcal { C } ( X )$ . Then $\varphi$ assumes finitely many non-zero values $a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n }$ . Let $A _ { i } = \varphi ^ { - 1 } ( a _ { i } )$ , which is a $\hat { G }$ -subset of $X$ . We define the integral of $\varphi$ by

$$
\int_ {X} \varphi (X) d x = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} a _ {i} \mu \left(A _ {i}\right).
$$

Given a map $f \colon X \to Y$ of $\hat { G }$ -sets, we define a push-forward map $f _ { * } \colon { \mathcal { C } } ( X ) \to { \mathcal { C } } ( Y )$ by integrating over the fibers of $f$ . We show that this has all the usual properties of a pushforward map (see §4.4).

1.3.3. Permutation representations. Suppose $\Gamma$ is a finite group. Given a finite $\Gamma$ -set $X$ , there is an associated permutation representation $k \lfloor X \rfloor$ . If $Y$ is a second finite $\Gamma$ -set, then the $k \lfloor \Gamma \rfloor$ -maps $k [ X ] \to k [ Y ]$ are given by $Y \times X$ matrices that are $\Gamma$ -invariant.

We wish to mimic the above picture to define a category ${ \underline { { \operatorname { P e r m } } } } ( G ; \mu )$ of “permutation representations.” For this, we need a theory of matrices. Let $X$ and $Y$ be finitary $G$ -sets. We define a $Y \times X$ matrix $A$ to be a Schwartz function $A \colon Y \times X \to k$ . Given a $Y \times X$ matrix $A$ and a $Z \times Y$ matrix $B$ , we define $B A$ to be the $Z \times X$ matrix given by

$$
(B A) (z, x) = \int_ {Y} B (z, y) A (y, x) d y.
$$

We show that this has the expected properties of matrix multiplication. We go on to study the trace of matrices in some detail. It is possible to extend many other concepts in linear algebra to this setting, such as Jordan decomposition, determinant, and characteristic polynomial; see [HS1, §7].

With this theory in hand, we can now define the category ${ \underline { { \operatorname { P e r m } } } } ( G ; \mu )$ . For each finitary $G$ -set $X$ there is an object $\operatorname { V e c } _ { X }$ , which one can think of as the space of column vectors indexed by $X$ ; a morphism $\mathrm { V e c } _ { X }  \mathrm { V e c } _ { Y }$ is a $G$ -invariant $Y \times X$ matrix; and composition

is given by matrix multiplication. This category is additive and carries a tensor product, which we denote by $\bigotimes$ . On objects, these operations are given by

$$
\operatorname {V e c} _ {X} \oplus \operatorname {V e c} _ {Y} = \operatorname {V e c} _ {X \mathrm {I I Y}}, \quad \operatorname {V e c} _ {X} \underline {{\otimes}} \operatorname {V e c} _ {Y} = \operatorname {V e c} _ {X \times Y}.
$$

On morphisms, these operations are given in the usual manner, namely block matrices and Kronecker products. We show that ${ \underline { { \operatorname { P e r m } } } } ( G ; \mu )$ is always a rigid tensor category; see §8.

$$
\left( \begin{array}{c c c c c} \alpha & \beta & \beta & \dots & \beta \\ \beta & \alpha & \beta & \dots & \beta \\ \beta & \beta & \alpha & \dots & \beta \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \beta & \beta & \beta & \dots & \alpha \end{array} \right)

1.3.4. General representations. The category ${ \underline { { \operatorname { P e r m } } } } ( G ; \mu )$ is essentially never abelian. We would therefore like to construct an abelian envelope of it.

To do this, we introduce the completed group algebra $A = A _ { k } ( G ; \mu )$ of $G$ . As a $k$ -module, $A$ is simply the inverse limit of Schwartz spaces ${ \mathcal { C } } ( G / U )$ over the open subgroups $U$ . The multiplication on $A$ is defined using convolution of functions (which uses integration, hence the dependence on $\mu$ ). We then define $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ; \mu )$ to be the category of “smooth” $A$ -modules; this condition simply means that the action of $A$ is continuous when the module is given the discrete topology. The Schwartz space ${ \mathcal { C } } ( X )$ carries the structure of a smooth $A$ -module, and these are the most important modules. The category $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ; \mu )$ is always a Grothendieck abelian category, and there is a canonical faithful functor

$$
\Phi \colon \underline {{\mathrm {P e r m}}} (G; \mu) \to \underline {{\mathrm {R e p}}} (G; \mu)
$$
which takes $\operatorname { V e c } _ { X }$ $X$ to ${ \mathcal { C } } ( X )$ . Assuming that $\mu$ is a normal measure (Definition 11.1), we show that $\Phi$ is also full.

We next define a tensor structure $\bigotimes$ on $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ; \mu )$ (assuming $\mu$ is normal). There is a “brute force” approach to this: namely, declare ${ \mathfrak { C } } ( X ) \otimes { \mathfrak { C } } ( Y ) = { \mathfrak { C } } ( X \times Y )$ and then extend to general modules by choosing presentations. We prefer to take a more organic approach. Let $M$ , $N$ , and $E$ be smooth $A$ -modules. A strongly bilinear map is a function

$$
q \colon M \times N \to E
$$
that is $k$ -bilinear, $G$ -equivariant, and satisfies the following additional condition: given $G$ -sets $X$ and $Y$ and Schwartz functions $\varphi \colon X \to M$ and $\psi \colon Y  N$ , we have

$$
q \left(\int_ {X} \varphi (x) d x, \int_ {Y} \psi (y) d y\right) = \int_ {X \times Y} q (\varphi (x), \psi (y)) d (x, y).
$$

Here we are integrating module-valued functions (see §11.9). The above condition essentially means that $q$ commutes with certain kinds of infinite sums. We define a tensor product to be an object equipped with a universal strongly bilinear map. We prove (Theorem 12.9) that

a tensor product always exists, and this endows $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ; \mu )$ with the structure of a tensor category.

Assume now that $k$ is a field. One of our main results (Theorem 13.2) states that if $\mu$ is quasi-regular and Propery (P) holds then $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ; \mu )$ is locally pre-Tannakian, and if $\mu$ is regular then $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ; \mu )$ is additionally semi-simple. See Definition 7.10 for Property (P), Definition 13.1 for locally pre-Tannakian, and §3.7 for (quasi-)regular. We also show (Theorem 13.13) that, in this setting, $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ; \mu )$ is the abelian envelope of Perm $( G ; \mu )$ in the precise sense of [CEAH]. See §1.5.2 for some discussion of the proofs.

1.4. Some examples. We now discuss some examples of oligomorphic groups, and what we can do with them. The first two examples are closely related to the categories of Deligne and Knop, while the next two are new.

1.4.1. The symmetric group. Recall that $\mathfrak { S }$ is the group of all permutations of $\Omega = \{ 1 , 2 , . . . \}$ . We show that $\Theta ( \mathfrak { S } )$ is the ring $\mathbf { Z } \langle x \rangle$ of integer-valued polynomials (Theorem 14.4). The $\mathbf { Z } \langle x \rangle$ - linear category $\underline { { \mathrm { P e r m } } } ( \mathfrak { S } ; \mu _ { \mathrm { u n i v } } )$ associated to the universal measure is very closely related to the category constructed in $\left[ \mathrm { H a r } \right]$ , and seems to be the “correct” integral version of Deligne’s interpolation category. The construction in [Har] worked with explicit bases (the Carter–Lusztig bases), and one of our initial sources of motivation was to find a basis-free construction of this category.

From the computation of $\Theta ( \mathfrak { S } )$ , we see that the measures $\mu _ { t }$ from Example 1.3 account for all $\mathbf { C }$ -valued measures for $\mathfrak { S }$ . We show that $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( \mathfrak { S } ; \mu _ { t } )$ is a locally pre-Tannakian category for all $t \in \mathbf { C }$ , and semi-simple for $t \not \in \mathbf { N }$ (Theorem 14.10). We also show that it is the abelian envelope of $\underline { { \mathrm { P e r m } } } ( \mathfrak { S } ; \mu _ { t } )$ . Results of Comes–Ostirk [CO2] imply that our category $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( \mathfrak { S } ; \mu _ { t } )$ agrees with Deligne’s abelian interpolation category $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ^ { \mathrm { a b } } ( \mathfrak { S } _ { t } )$ constructed in [Del3, Proposition 8.19].

The computation of $\Theta ( \mathfrak { S } )$ also shows that measures valued in a field $k$ of characteristic $p$ are parametrized by $\mathbf { Z } _ { p }$ . This was one of the main points of $\left[ \mathrm { H a r } \right]$ , and is consistent with the idea of $^ { 6 6 } p$ -adic dimension” of tensor categories, as studied in [EHO]. These measures are not normal, and our $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( \mathfrak { S } ; \mu )$ categories are not well-behaved in this setting (see §14.7).

1.4.2. Linear groups. Let $\mathbf { F }$ be a finite field with $q$ elements and let $\begin{array} { r } { G = \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } \mathbf { G } \mathbf { L } _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } ) } \end{array}$ . The group $G$ acts oligomorphically on $\mathbf { V } = \textstyle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } \mathbf { F } ^ { n }$ . We show that $\Theta ( G )$ is a $q$ -analog of the ring of integer-valued polynomials (Theorem 15.7), which is closely related to the rings studied in [HH]. In particular, $\Theta ( G ) \otimes \mathbf { Q } = \mathbf { Q } [ x ]$ , and so for each $t \in \mathbf { C }$ there is an associated complex-valued measure $\mu _ { t }$ .

We show that $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ; \mu _ { t } )$ is a locally pre-Tannakian category for all $t \in \mathbf { C }$ , and semi-simple for $t \not \in { \bf N } _ { q }$ (Theorem 15.15); here $\mathbf { N } _ { q }$ denotes the set of non-negative $q$ -integers. The case $t \not \in { \bf N } _ { q }$ had previously been studied by Knop [Kno1, Kno2], and we rely on his results in this case (though this dependence could probably be excised). The case $t \in \mathbf { N } _ { q }$ appears to be new, though we have been informed that Entova-Aizenbud and Heidersdorf have results in this direction related to their forthcoming work [EAH].

The group $G$ also acts oligomorphically on $\mathbf { V } \oplus \mathbf { V } _ { * }$ , where $\mathbf { V } _ { * }$ is the restricted dual of $\mathbf { V }$ , and this leads to a second topology on $G$ . We write $G ^ { p }$ (resp. $G ^ { \ell }$ ) for the topological group associated to the action on $\mathbf { V }$ (resp. $\mathbf { V } \oplus \mathbf { V } _ { * }$ ). We show that $\Theta ( G ^ { \ell } ) = \Theta ( G ^ { p } )$ . We suspect that $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ^ { \ell } ; \mu _ { t } )$ and $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ^ { p } ; \mu _ { t } )$ are equivalent for generic values of $t$ , and differ at a countable set of values. See §15.6 for more details.

text: 1.4.3. Homeomorphisms of the line and circle. Let ${ \cal G } = \mathrm { A u t } ( { \bf R } , < )$ be the group of orderpreserving bijections of the real line, which is oligomorphic with respect to its action on $\mathbf { R }$ . The $\hat { G }$ -subsets of $\mathbf { R }$ are finite unions of points and open intervals. More generally, a finitary $\hat { G }$ -set $X$ is a finite disjoint union of finite products of open intervals; in particular, $X$ is naturally a smooth manifold. We show that one obtains a $\mathbf { Z }$ -valued measure $\mu$ by taking $\mu ( X )$ to be the compactly supported Euler characteristic of $X$ . Our theory of integration in this case amounts to the Euler calculus introduced by Schapira and Viro (see, e.g., [Vir]).

For a field $k$ (of any characteristic), we show that the category $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } _ { k } ( G ; \mu )$ is locally pre-Tannakian and semi-simple (Theorem 16.10). The standard permutation module in this category has dimension $- 1$ . This is the first example of a semi-simple rigid tensor category in positive characteristic that is not of moderate growth. We prove that $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } _ { k } ( G ; \mu )$ cannot be obtained by interpolating representation categories of finite groups (Theorem 16.11).

In fact, there are three other $\mathbf { Z }$ -valued measures for $G$ , though they are not as well-behaved as $\mu$ (e.g., we do not construct pre-Tannakian categories associated to them). In all, these four measures define a ring isomorphism $\Theta ( G ) = \mathbf { Z } ^ { 4 }$ (Theorem 16.7). Conceptually, the four measures correspond to the four partial compactifications of $\mathbf { R }$ .

There is a similar story associated to the group of orientation-preserving self-homeomorphisms of the unit circle S (see §16.8). In this case, we again obtain a pre-Tannakian category, but it is no longer semi-simple.

1.4.4. Boron trees. A boron tree is a finite tree in which internal vertices have valence three. An example is depicted in Figure 2; see also §17. The internal vertices are called “boron atoms” and the leaves are called “hydrogen atoms.” Given a boron tree $T$ , one can define a quaternary relation $R$ on the set $T _ { H }$ of hydrogen atoms by declaring $R ( w , x ; y , z )$ to be true if the geodesic joining $w$ and $x$ meets the one joining $y$ and $z$ . It is really this relation that is of interest, though it is equivalent to the tree structure.

Let $\mathbf { T } ( \mathbf { Q } _ { 2 } )$ be the Bruhat–Tits tree for $\mathbf { S L } _ { 2 } ( \mathbf { Q } _ { 2 } )$ ; see [Ser1, Chapter 2] for a picture of this object and more discussion. This is essentially an infinite boron tree: the boron atoms are the unimodular $\mathbf { Z } _ { 2 }$ -lattices in $\mathbf { Q } _ { 2 } ^ { 2 }$ and the hydrogen atoms are the lines in $\mathbf { Q } _ { 2 } ^ { 2 }$ (these really constitute the boundary of the tree). The quaternary relation in this case can be described as follows: $R ( w , x ; y , z )$ holds if the cross-ration of the four points $w , x , y , z \in \mathbf { P } ^ { 1 } ( \mathbf { Q } _ { 2 } )$ reduces modulo 2 to $\infty \in \mathbf { P } ^ { 1 } ( \mathbf { F } _ { 2 } )$ .

Let $F$ be a dense subfield of $\begin{array} { r } { \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } \mathbf { Q } _ { 2 } ( 2 ^ { 1 / n } ) } \end{array}$ of countable cardinality, and consider the analogous tree $\mathbf { T } ( F )$ . This is like the Bruhat–Tits tree, except it branches in a dense fashion and has countable boundary. The tree $\mathbf { T } ( F )$ is the Fra¨ıss´e limit of the class of finite boron trees (see §6.2.5). Let $G$ be the group of all permutations of the hydrogen atoms in $\mathbf { T } ( F )$
OLIGOMORPHIC GROUPS AND TENSOR CATEGORIES

preserving the quaternary relation $R$ . This is an oligomorphic group. This construction— producing an oligomorphic group as the automorphism group of a Fra¨ıss´e limit—is how most oligomorphic groups arise.

We show (Theorem 17.6) that a “relative” version of $\Theta ( G )$ is the ring $\mathbf { Z } [ x ] / ( 2 x ^ { 2 } + x )$ , which essentially means that there are two measures $\mu$ and $\nu$ . We do not compute $\Theta ( G )$ completely, but one should be able to by building on our work. For any field $k$ of characteristic $\neq 2 , 3$ , we construct a semi-simple pre-Tannakian category over $k$ associated to $G$ and $\mu$ (Theorem 17.10). The standard permutation module in this category has dimension $\frac { 3 } { 2 }$ .
1.5. Additional aspects. We have now discussed the main constructions and examples of this paper. However, there are a number of additional pieces of material that merit comment. We now discuss them.

1.5.1. Model theory. Oligomorphic groups are closely connected to model theory. Given some class $\mathfrak { A }$ of finite structures, such as totally ordered sets, graphs, or boron trees, one can sometimes form the Fra¨ıss´e limit, which is a suitably universal countable structure $\Omega$ containing each member of $\mathfrak { A }$ . The automorphism group of the Fra¨ıss´e limit is often oligomorphic, and this is the most important construction of oligomorphic groups.

Suppose we have an oligomorphic group $G$ obtained as above, i.e., $G = \mathrm { A u t } ( \Omega )$ where $\Omega$ is the Fra¨ıss´e limit of some class $\mathfrak { A }$ . Since $G$ is completely determined from $\mathfrak { A }$ , one should be able to “see” measures for $G$ on the $\mathfrak { A }$ side. We explain how this works in §6. Precisely, we define a notion of measure for the class $\mathfrak { A }$ , and show that these measures essentially correspond to measures for $G$ (Theorem 6.9); in fact, there is a slight subtlety here in that one actually gets measures for $G$ relative to a stabilizer class $\mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { O } }$ (see §2.6 below).

One of the advantages of this perspective is that it can be much easier to think about measures on the $\mathfrak { A }$ side. For example, suppose $\mathfrak { A }$ is the class of boron trees. A (regular) measure for $\mathfrak { A }$ is a rule assigning to each boron tree a number, such that some concrete identities hold. This is much easier to work with than the corresponding notion of measure for $G$ , since the open subgroups of $G$ are not obvious. We therefore take the $\mathfrak { A }$ approach when we analyzing measures in §17.

Another advantage of this perspective is that one can apply general ideas from model theory to the study of measures. For example, we show (Theorem 6.24) that if the class $\mathfrak { A }$ is smoothly approximable then it admits a measure. We note that the smoothly approximable condition has received significant attention in the literature [CH, KLM]. The smoothly approximable case seems to roughly coincide with previously known interpolation categories; e.g., it includes the categories of Deligne and Knop.

1.5.2. Abelian envelopes, nilpotent matrices, and Property ( $P$ ). We have already mentioned one of our main results, Theorem 13.2, which states that if $\mu$ is quasi-regular and satisfies Property (P) then $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ; \mu )$ is the abelian envelope of $\underline { { \mathrm { P e r m } } } ( G ; \mu )$ . We now say a little bit more about what goes into the proof of this, and what role Property (P) has.

We can pass to an open subgroup of $G$ to assume that the measure is regular. The problem is then to show that endomorphism algebras in Perm $( G ; \mu )$ are semi-simple. Deligne and Knop accomplish this by connecting these algebras to group algebras, but this approach does not seem viable in general. Regularity implies that the trace pairings on endomorphism algebras are non-degenerate (Proposition 7.18). So to obtain semi-simplicity, it thus suffices to show that nilpotent matrices have trace zero. This is really the key problem.
NATE HARMAN AND ANDREW SNOWDEN

We show that nilpotent matrices always have vanishing trace in positive characteristic (Corollary 7.9). This does not require any assumption at all on $\mu$ , but relies on an important lifting property for measures (see §1.5.4). From this, we deduce the same is true over general coefficient rings, provided $\mu$ satisfies Property (P) (Theorem 7.11). Property (P) essentially means that $\mu$ can be reduced modulo enough primes, and this allows us to transport the result back from positive characteristic. We note that quasi-regularity is not needed here.

In the case of the symmetric group, we show that all measures satisfy (P); this actually requires a non-trivial number theoretic argument (see §14.5). We thereby recover results of Comes–Ostrik [CO2] that Deligne’s category admits an abelian envelope. In the case of Knop’s interpolation category $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( \mathbf G \mathbf L _ { t } ( \mathbf F _ { q } ) )$ , the situation is curious. At the singular parameter values, it is easy to see that (P) holds, and our theory produces an abelian envelope; this was not previously known. At the regular parameter values, Property (P) is quite subtle and seems to be closely related to the Artin primitive root conjecture (see Remark 15.16). We expect (P) holds, but we cannot prove it. However, Knop had already shown that the Karoubi envelope gives the abelian envelope in this case. In the case of $\operatorname { A u t } ( \mathbf { Q } , < )$ and boron trees, it is quite straightforward to see that (P) holds.

We make two additional remarks in this direction. First, in [Sn3], the second author constructs two regular Q-valued measures $\mu$ and $\nu$ on a particular oligomorphic group, neither of which satisfy (P). For $\mu$ nilpotent matrices have trace zero, but for $\nu$ this is not the case. This shows that (P) is not necessary for nilpotents to have trace zero, but also that the condition is not entirely artificial. And second, if $\mu$ is not normal then the problem of constructing an abelian envelope of ${ \underline { { \operatorname { P e r m } } } } ( G ; \mu )$ seems to be quite difficult; in this case, we do not even have a natural candidate.

1.5.3. Linearizations. Fix an oligomorphic group $G$ and let $\mathcal { S } ( G )$ be the category of finitary $G$ -sets. We define a linearization of $\mathcal { S } ( G )$ to be a $k$ -linear tensor category $\mathbb { T }$ having the same objects as $\mathcal { S } ( G )$ , and where disjoint union and cartesian product in $\mathcal { S } ( G )$ become direct sum and tensor product in $\mathbb { T }$ . The precise definition (Definition 9.8) is a bit more involved, but it is important to note that the definition of linearization does not refer to the concept of measure. The basic example of a linearization is the category ${ \underline { { \operatorname { P e r m } } } } ( G ; \mu )$ .

A natural question is whether the categories ${ \underline { { \operatorname { P e r m } } } } ( G ; \mu )$ account for all linearizations as $\mu$ varies. Theorem 9.9 answers this in the affirmative. As a corollary, we obtain a moduli-theoretic (and equation-free) interpretation of $\Theta ( G )$ : its spectrum is the space of linearizations. This result plays an important role in [HS4].

1.5.4. $\Theta ( G )$ is a binomial ring. Recall that a binomial ring is a commutative ring that is torsion-free as an abelian group and closed under the operation $x \mapsto { \binom { x } { n } }$ for all $n \geq 0$ . The deepest result we prove about $\Theta ( G )$ for a general group $G$ is Theorem 5.1, which states that $\Theta ( G )$ is a binomial ring. This theorem has strong consequences for measures. For instance, it implies that any measure valued in a field of positive characteristic $p$ in fact takes values in the prime subfield $\mathbf { F } _ { p }$ , and lifts uniquely to $\mathbf { Z } _ { p }$ . To prove Theorem 5.1, we show that $\Theta ( G )$ admits a $\lambda$ -ring structure with trivial Adam’s operations, which implies the result by a theorem of Elliott [Eli].
1.6. Relation to previous work. Our work connects to much previous work:

• The most important connection is to the theory of oligomorphic groups and homogeneous structures. Our framework enables one to import ideas from this area into the theory of tensor categories. We refer to [Mac] for a detailed overview of homogeneous
OLIGOMORPHIC GROUPS AND TENSOR CATEGORIES

structures. We note that certain kinds of measures (or Euler characteristics) have appeared in the model theory literature, e.g., [AMSW, KS, Wol]. While these are similar to ours in some ways, they are not exactly the same.

list_items: • Our work obviously owes a debt to Deligne’s paper [Del3], but the most direct antecedent is Knop’s paper [Kno2]. Knop defines a notion of degree function on a category, and uses this to construct tensor categories. This is at least superficially similar to how we define a notion of measure on the category $\mathcal { S } ( G )$ of finitary $G$ -sets, and use this to construct tensor categories. However, there are a number of important differences, e.g., Knop’s theory does not accommodate groups like $\operatorname { A u t } ( \mathbf { R } , < )$ . The two theories are compared in detail in [Sn4], and it is shown that all of Knop’s tensor categories can be constructed using the framework of this paper.

• An important topic in interpolation categories is the construction of abelian envelopes. In this direction, we recover the results of [CO2, Del3] for $\mathfrak { S }$ , and establish complementary results to [Kno2] for ${ \bf G L } _ { \infty } ( { \bf F } _ { q } )$ . Moreover, we describe the abelian envelopes in these cases (and others) in a concrete manner, as modules over the completed group algebra. We make use of [CEAH] for a precise definition and characterization of abelian envelopes.

• The paper [EHO] shows that in a nice enough tensor category over a field of characteristic $p$ , objects can be assigned a $p$ -adic dimension. This principle is echoed in our work in a few places, such as the lifting result for measures discussed in §1.5.4.
• The smooth representation theory of oligomorphic groups is studied in [Nek1]. Some cases are also treated in [DLLX].

text: 1.7. Subsequent work. Since the first version of this paper was posted, a number of subsequent works have appeared building on it. We discuss some of these here.

1.7.1. Discrete pre-Tannakian categories. Define a pre-Tannakian category $\mathcal { C }$ to be discrete if every object is a quotient of an ´etale algebra in $\mathcal { C }$ . Note that if $G$ is an algebraic group then ${ \mathrm { R e p } } ( G )$ is discrete if and only if $G$ is a finite group. In [HS4], we show that every discrete pre-Tannakian category has the form $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ; \mu )$ for some (pro-)oligomorphic group $G$ and measure $\mu$ . This shows that oligomorphic groups are intrinsically connected to pre-Tannakian categories. In particular, the categories constructed in this paper account for a very natural piece of the pre-Tannakian landscape.

We say a few words about the proof of the theorem from [HS4], as it connects to some ideas in this paper. Many of the constructions in this paper really depend only on the category $\mathcal { S } ( G )$ of finitary $G$ -sets, and not on $G$ itself. It is therefore natural to characterize this class of categories. We do this in [HS3]. We define a class of categories called $B$ -categories, and a more restrictive class called pre-Galois categories. We show that pre-Galois categories are exactly those of the form $\mathcal { S } ( G )$ for some pro-oligomorphic group $G$ . More general Bcategories are also of interest, as the constructions in this paper apply to them as well; for instance, they encompass the “relative” situation discussed in §2.6.

Suppose now that $\mathcal { C }$ is any pre-Tannakian category. In [HS4], we show that the opposite category of ´etale algebras in $\mathrm { { \small ~  ~ } }$ is pre-Galois, and thus of the form $\mathcal { S } ( G )$ for some prooligomorphic group $G$ . We define $G$ to be the oligomorphic fundamental group of $\mathcal { C }$ ; this should be the component group of a more comprehensive fundamental group. We show that $G$ comes with a canonical measure $\mu$ ; this makes crucial use of the results of §9 in this paper. If $\mathcal { C }$ is discrete, we then show that it is equivalent to $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ; \mu )$ .
NATE HARMAN AND ANDREW SNOWDEN

1.7.2. Algebraic representations. Deligne and Milne [DM] defined a category $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( \mathbf { G L } _ { t } )$ that interpolates the representation categories of the algebraic groups $\mathbf { G L } _ { n }$ . This category is not associated to an oligomorphic group; it is not discrete. From the perspective of this paper, this category should arise from some kind of measure on the infinite dimensional algebraic group $\mathbf { G L } _ { \infty }$ $\infty$ . More generally, one might hope for a theory of measures and tensor categories associated to “algebraic–oligomorphic” groups.

With this idea in mind, we defined a notion of algebraic–oligomorphic group in [HS2]. We also constructed many non-trivial examples, using a variant of Fra¨ıss´e limits. For example, for $d \geq 1$ , define a $d$ -space to be a vector space equipped with a symmetric $d$ -multilinear form. We show that there is a universal homogeneous $d$ -space (over $\mathbf { C }$ , say). Its automorphism group $G _ { d }$ is algebraic-oligomorphic. The group $G _ { 2 }$ is the infinite orthogonal group, while $G _ { 3 }$ is a kind of cubic analog of it. We have not yet determined the right notion of measure on these groups. We see this as a very important open problem.

1.7.3. The Delannoy category. Let $G$ be the group $\mathrm { A u t } ( { \bf R } , < )$ . As discussed in §1.4.3, we construct a semi-simple pre-Tannakian $\mathcal { C }$ associated to $G$ in this paper. In a follow-up paper [HSS1], we study this category in great detail. We name it the Delannoy category, since it can be described combinatorially in terms of Delannoy paths. We find that the Delannoy category has many special properties: for example, all the simple objects have categorical dimension $\pm 1$ , and the Adams operations act trivially on its Grothendieck group. In another paper [HSS2], we study the circular analog of the Delannoy category. This case is somewhat more complicated since it is not semi-simple.
1.7.4. Other examples. The theory developed in this paper has been applied to a few more oligomorphic groups:

list_items: (a) In [HNS], we extend our work on boron trees (§17) to trees with valence $\leq n$ , or trees of unbounded valence. In the bounded valence case, we find two measures, one of which leads to a semi-simple pre-Tannakian category $\mathbb { D } ( n )$ . In the unbounded case, we find two one-parameter families of measures. One of these leads to a one-parameter family $\mathcal { C } ( t )$ of semi-simple pre-Tannakian categories (away from a countable set of singular parameters). The category $\mathcal { C } ( t )$ can be viewed as the Deligne interpolation of the categories $\mathbb { D } ( n )$ . This is the first non-trivial example of interpolation where the initial categories are of superexponential growth.

(b) In [Sn3], the homeomorphism group of the Cantor set is studied. There are two measures $\mu$ and $
u$ . The measure $\mu$ leads to a semi-simple pre-Tannakian category of doubly exponential growth, which was the first such example. The measure $
u$ is regular, but the category $\underline { { \mathrm { P e r m } } } ( G ; 
u )$ has nilpotent endomorphisms with non-zero trace; thus it does not embed into a pre-Tannakian category. This was the first such example, and shows that something like our Property (P) is necessary.

(c) S. Kriz [Kri] considers the semi-direct product of $\operatorname { A u t } ( \mathbf { Q } , < )$ with the Borel subgroup in an appropriate version of ${ \bf G L } _ { \infty } ( { \bf F } _ { q } )$ . She constructs a semi-simple pre-Tannakian category associated to this group, aways from finitely many bad characteristics. This is the fastest-growing known pre-Tannakian category in positive characteristic, and (in combination with [Sn2]) leads to the fastest-growing known pre-Tannakian category in characteristic 0.
(d) Fix a $d$ -coloring on the unit circle S in which every color is dense, and let $G$ be the (oligomorphic) group of permutations of $\mathbf { S }$ preserving the cyclic order and coloring.

(e) In [Sn5], the second author studies measures for permutations (finite sets equipped with two total orders), and finds that there are exactly 37 measures.

text: 1.8. The first version of this paper. The first version of this paper [HS1] is available on the arxiv. It is somewhat longer than this version: it contains some proofs we have omitted here, many additional tangential comments, and some material that we have chosen to exclude from this version (such as the discussion of Farahat–Higman algebras). We sometimes cite this first version to point to additional details. We note that what we now call “pro-oligomorphic groups” were called “admissible groups” in the first version.
1.9. Where to go from here. Our work presents a multitude of problems to study. However, there are two main directions we wish to highlight as particularly important.

The first is to understand the ring $\Theta ( G )$ better. We have only succeeded in computing $\Theta ( G )$ in a handful of cases, and each one is rather laborious. And we have been unable to even determine if $\Theta ( G )$ is non-zero in some cases, such as when $G$ is the automorphism group of the Rado graph. We would therefore like some tools for working with these rings.

The second direction concerns abelian envelopes. Our results on ${ \underline { { \operatorname { P e r m } } } } ( G ; \mu )$ are consistent with it having an abelian envelope (see Remark 8.13) in many cases. When the measure $\mu$ is quasi-regular and (P) holds, we show that $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ; \mu )$ is the abelian envelope. However, we say nothing outside of this case. Can abelian envelopes be constructed more generally?
1.10. Notation and conventions. There are a few important definitions and conventions we mention here:

list_items: • For a pro-oligomorphic group $G$ , we use the term “ $G$ -set” to mean “a set equipped with a smooth action of $G$ .” See §2.3.

• A tensor category is a $k$ -linear additive symmetric monoidal category such that the monoidal product is $k$ -bilinear. We denote the unit object by 1. A tensor functor is a $k$ -linear symmetric monoidal functor.
• A rigid tensor category is one in which all objects are rigid, i.e., possess a dual; see §8.4. The notion of (locally) pre-Tannakian category is given in Definition 13.1.

Part I. Integration on oligomorphic groups
2. Oligomorphic groups
2.1. Oligomorphic groups. We begin by restating the following fundamental definition:
Definition 2.1. An oligomorphic group is a group $G$ with a given faithful action on a set $\Omega$ such that $G$ has finitely many orbits on $\Omega ^ { n }$ for all $n \geq 0$ . 

We refer to Cameron’s book [Cam3] for general background on oligomorphic groups. The “finitely many orbits” condition appears so ubiquitously in this paper that it will be convenient to give it a name: we say that an action of a group $G$ on a set $\Omega$ is finitary if $G$ has finitely many orbits on $\Omega$ , or equivalently, the quotient set $G \backslash \Omega$ is finite. Thus in the oligomorphic condition, we require that $\Omega ^ { n }$ is finitary for all $n \geq 0$ .

For a set $\Omega$ , let $\Omega ^ { [ n ] }$ be the subset of $\Omega ^ { n }$ consisting of points with distinct coordinates, and let $\Omega ^ { ( n ) }$ be the set of $n$ -element subsets of $\Omega$ . If $G$ acts on $\Omega$ then it is easy to see that the finitary conditions for $\Omega ^ { n }$ , $\Omega ^ { [ n ] }$ , and $\Omega ^ { ( n ) }$ are equivalent. Thus oligomorphic could equivalently be defined using $\Omega ^ { \left[ n \right] }$ or $\Omega ^ { ( n ) }$ in place of $\Omega ^ { n }$ .
Model theory provides a wealth of examples of oligomorphic groups, and, in a sense, explains the oligomorphic condition. We discuss this in §6. For now, we content ourselves with a few examples.
Example 2.2. We give a number of examples of oligomorphic groups.

list_items: (a) The infinite symmetric group $\mathfrak { S }$ is oligomorphic (with respect to its defining action). For our purposes, it does not really matter which version of $\mathfrak { S }$ one uses, but to be definite we take $\mathfrak { S }$ to be the group of all permutations of the positive integers.

(b) Let $\mathbf { F }$ be a finite field and let $\mathbf { V } = \bigoplus _ { i \geq 1 } \mathbf { F } e _ { i }$ be a vector space over $\mathbf { F }$ of countable infinite dimension. Then the group $G = \textstyle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } \mathbf { G } \mathbf { L } _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ is oligomorphic, with respect to the action on $\mathbf { V }$ . Let $\mathbf { V } _ { * } = \oplus _ { i \geq 1 } \mathbf { F } e _ { i } ^ { * }$ be the restricted dual of $\mathbf { V }$ . Then $G$ is also oligomorphic with respect to its action on $\mathbf { V } \oplus \mathbf { V } _ { * }$ , and this leads to a different theory (see Example 2.6). The infinite orthogonal, symplectic, and unitary groups over $\mathbf { F }$ are also oligomorphic.

list_items: (c) The group $\mathrm { A u t } ( { \bf R } , < )$ of orientation-preserving homeomorphisms of the real line is oligomorphic (acting on $\mathbf { R }$ ). A similar example is $\operatorname { A u t } ( \mathbf { Q } , < )$ , the group of orderpreserving permutations of the rational numbers. These two examples are essentially equivalent; we prefer working with the former, though the latter appears more often in the oligomorphic group literature. There are some similar examples: e.g., one can consider homeomorphisms of $\mathbf { R }$ that may not preserve the orientation, or replace the real line with the circle.

(d) Let $G$ be the group of self-homeomorphisms of the Cantor set. This group acts oligomorphically on the set of clopen subsets of the Cantor set. The theory developed in this paper is studied for this group in [Sn3].

(e) Let $R$ be the Rado graph. There are many ways to think about this graph. It is the Fra¨ıss´e limit of the class of finite graphs. It is also the random countable graph in the sense of Erd˝os–R´enyi [ER]. The automorphism group $\operatorname { A u t } ( R )$ of $R$ is oligomorphic, with respect to its action on the vertex set $\Omega$ of $R$ . The orbits of $\operatorname { A u t } ( R )$ on $\Omega ^ { ( n ) }$ are in bijection with isomorphism classes of graphs on $n$ vertices. There are several similar examples, e.g., using bipartite graphs or $K _ { n }$ -free graphs.

(f) There are a number of variants of the above constructions. One can consider products (such as $\mathfrak { S } \times \mathfrak { S }$ acting on $\Omega \amalg \Omega$ ) and wreath products (such as $\mathfrak { S } \wr \mathfrak { S }$ acting on $\Omega \times \Omega$ , or $\mathfrak { S } \wr \Gamma$ acting on $\Gamma ^ { \Omega }$ , with $\Gamma$ a finite group). One can add colorings, e.g., 2-color $\mathbf { Q }$ and consider permutations which preserve the order and the color. There is also a way to combine certain examples, e.g., one can combine $\operatorname { A u t } ( \mathbf { Q } , < )$ and the automorphism group of the Rado graph; see [BPP]. 

text: 2.2. Pro-oligomorphic groups. Oligomorphic groups admit a natural topology which will be very useful for us. To speak about it, we introduce some terminology. Recall that a topological group $G$ is non-archimedean if its open subgroups form a neighborhood basis of the identity, and Roelcke precompact if whenever $U$ and $V$ are non-empty open subsets of $G$ there exists a finite subset $S$ of $G$ such that $G = U S V$ . We note that if $G$ is non-archimedean then $G$ is Hausdorff if and only if the intersection of all open subgroups is trivial, and $G$ is Roelcke precompact if and only if for all open subgroups $U$ and $V$ the double coset space $U \backslash G / V$ is finite.
Definition 2.3. A pro-oligomorphic group $^ 3$ is a topological group that is Hausdorff, nonarchimedean, and Roelcke precompact. 
One easily sees that any open subgroup of a pro-oligomorphic group is pro-oligomorphic, when given the subspace topology. This will be used constantly in what follows.

Example 2.5. Let $\mathfrak { S }$ be the infinite symmetric group acting on $\Omega = \{ 1 , 2 , . . . \}$ . Define ${ \mathfrak { S } } ( n )$ to be the subgroup of $\mathfrak { S }$ consisting of permutations that fix each of the numbers $1 , \ldots , n$ . Then a subgroup of $\mathfrak { S }$ is open if and only if it contains ${ \mathfrak { S } } ( n )$ for some $n$ . Example 2.6. Consider the infinite general linear group $G$ acting on $\mathbf { V }$ (see Example 2.2). We define the parabolic topology on $G$ to be the one induced from its action on $\mathbf { V }$ . The fundamental open subgroups for this topology have the form

$$
\left[ \begin{array}{c c} 1 _ {n} & * \\ 0 & * \end{array} \right].
$$
We define the Levi topology on $G$ to be the one induced from its action on $\mathbf { V } \oplus \mathbf { V } _ { * }$ . The fundamental open subgroups for this topology have the form

$$
\left[ \begin{array}{c c} 1 _ {n} & 0 \\ 0 & * \end{array} \right].
$$
We thus see that $G$ carries two distinct pro-oligomorphic topologies. These examples are discussed further in §15. 

The groups of primary interest to us in this paper occur as oligomorphic groups. However, the theory we develop only depends on the topology, and not the defining permutation action. For this reason, we work with pro-oligomorphic groups throughout. We note that there are pro-oligomorphic groups which are not oligomorphic, such as infinite profinite groups.

2.4. Induction. Let $U$ be an open subgroup of a pro-oligomorphic group $G$ and let $X$ be a $U$ -set. We define the induction of $U$ , denoted $I _ { U } ^ { G } ( X )$ , to be the set $G \times ^ { U } \ X$ ; this is the quotient of the product $G \times X$ by the relations $( g u , x ) = ( g , u x )$ for $g \in G$ , $u \in U$ , and $x \in X$ . The group $G$ acts on $I _ { U } ^ { G } ( X )$ through its action on the first factor: $g \cdot ( g ^ { \prime } , x ) = ( g g ^ { \prime } , x )$ . One readily verifies that this action is smooth, and so $I _ { U } ^ { G } ( X )$ is a $G$ -set. We have the following additional properties, whose verification we leave to the reader:

list_items: • There is a well-defined map of $G$ -sets $I _ { U } ^ { G } ( X ) \to G / U$ given by $( g , x ) \mapsto g$ , the fiber of which over $1 \in G / U$ is naturally identified with $X$ .
• We have a natural bijection $G \backslash I _ { U } ^ { G } ( X ) \cong U \backslash X$ .
• If $X$ is a finitary $U$ -set then $I _ { U } ^ { G } ( X )$ is a finitary $G$ -set.

text: 2.5. Infinitesimal actions. Fix a pro-oligomorphic group $G$ . It will often be convenient to work with $U$ -sets, for $U$ an open subgroup of $G$ , without having to specify $U$ explicitly. We now introduce a device that allows us to do so.

A $\hat { G }$ -action on a set $X$ is an action of some open subgroup $U$ of $G$ . The subgroup $U$ is called a group of definition for the action. Shrinking the group of definition does not change the $\hat { G }$ -action. Formally, a $\hat { G }$ -action is an element of the set li $\mu _ { U C G } A ( U , X )$ , where the direct limit is taken over the open subgroups $U$ of $G$ , and $A ( U , X )$ denotes the set of all actions of $U$ on $X$ . It is important to note that $\hat { G }$ is simply a piece of notation and not a mathematical object. However, at an intuitive level, we think of $\hat { G }$ as an infinitesimal neighborhood of the identity in $G$ .

Consider a set $X$ equipped with a $\hat { G }$ -action. We say that the action is smooth if the action of $U$ is smooth for some group of definition $U$ ; one easily sees that this is independent of the choice of $U$ . We only consider smooth $\hat { G }$ -actions, and so, as in Convention 2.7, we define a $\hat { G }$ -set to be a set equipped with a smooth $\hat { G }$ -action.

Let $X$ be a $\hat { G }$ -set. We say that $X$ is finitary if it is finitary as a $U$ -set for some group of definition $U$ ; this is well-defined (i.e., independent of the choice of $U$ ) by Proposition 2.8(c). A subset $Y$ of $X$ is a $\hat { G }$ -subset if there is a group of definition $U$ for $X$ that leaves $Y$ stable. Every finite subset $Y$ of $X$ is a $\hat { G }$ -subset: indeed, $Y$ is stable under the open subgroup $G ( Y )$ that fixes each element of $Y$ . It is clear that the collection of $\hat { G }$ -subsets of $X$ is closed under

2.6. The relative setting. Let $G$ be a pro-oligomorphic group. A stabilizer class in $G$ is a collection $\mathcal { E } ^ { \sigma }$ of open subgroups satisfying the following conditions:

list_items: (a) $\mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { O } }$ contains $G$ .
(b) $\mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { O } }$ is stable under conjugation.
(c) $\mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { O } }$ is stable under finite intersections.
(d) $\mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { O } }$ is a neighborhood basis for the identity.

text: If $G$ is oligomorphic then the collection of all stabilizer groups on $\Omega ^ { n }$ , as $n$ varies, forms a stabilizer class; we call this the stabilizer class generated by $\Omega$ .

Fix a stabilizer class $\mathcal { E } ^ { \sigma }$ . We say that a $G$ -set is $\mathcal { E } ^ { \sigma }$ -smooth if the stabilizer of every element of $X$ belongs to $\mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { O } }$ . More generally, if $U$ is an open subgroup of $G$ (not necessarily in $\mathcal { E } ^ { \sigma }$ ), we say that a $U$ -set is $\mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { O } }$ -smooth if the stabilizer of every element has the form $U \cap V$ for some $V \in \mathcal { E } ^ { \circ }$ . This leads to a notion of $\mathcal { E } ^ { \circ }$ -smoothness for $\hat { G }$ -sets. The class of ${ \mathcal { E } } ^ { \omega } .$ -smooth sets (for $G$ , $U$ , or $\hat { G }$ ) is stable under finite products and co-product, fiber products, and passing to stable subsets. Thus the category of $\mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { O } }$ -smooth $G$ -sets formally resembles the category of $G$ -sets in many ways.

Most of our work with pro-oligomorphic groups extends to the setting of pro-oligomorphic groups equipped with a stabilizer class; we refer to this as the “relative setting.” To keep exposition simple, we do our main work in the absolute setting, and then sometimes comment on generalizations to the relative setting.

3. Measures

3.1. Overview. Fix a pro-oligomorphic group $G$ and a commutative ring $k$ for the duration of §3. In this section, we introduce a notion of measure for $G$ . This definition is one of the key ideas in this paper. As we explain in §4, a measure allows one to develop a theory of integration, which in turn allows us to define tensor categories; thus everything rests on measures. We also introduce the ring $\Theta ( G )$ which carries the universal measure for $G$ . The results in this section give various ways of describing $\Theta ( G )$ , each of which will be used subsequently.
3.2. Measures. The following is the key definition:

Definition 3.1. A measure for $G$ with values in $k$ is a rule $\mu$ that assigns to every finitary $\hat { G }$ -set $X$ a quantity $\mu ( X )$ in $k$ such that the following conditions hold (in which $X$ and $Y$ are finitary $\hat { G }$ -sets):

list_items: (a) If $X$ and $Y$ are isomorphic then $\mu ( X ) = \mu ( Y )$ .
(b) We have $\mu ( \mathbf { 1 } ) = 1$ , where $\mathbf { 1 }$ is the one-point set.
(c) We have $\mu ( X \amalg Y ) = \mu ( X ) + \mu ( Y )$ .
(d) For $g \in G$ , we have $\mu ( X ) = \mu ( X ^ { g } )$ , where $X ^ { g }$ is the conjugate of $X$ by $g$

(e) If $X$ and $Y$ are transitive $U$ -sets, for some open subgroup $U$ , and $X  Y$ is a map of $U$ -sets with fiber $F ^ { \prime }$ (over some point), then $\mu ( X ) = \mu ( F ) \cdot \mu ( Y )$ . 

text: Remark 3.2. We make a number of remarks concerning this definition:

list_items: (a) We elaborate on condition (3.1e). Let $f \colon X \to Y$ be the map, and suppose that $F = f ^ { - 1 } ( y )$ for $y \in Y$ . First note that $F ^ { \prime }$ is a $\hat { G }$ -subset of $X$ : indeed, it is stable under the stabilizer of $y$ in $U$ . Second, suppose that $F ^ { \prime } = f ^ { - 1 } ( y ^ { \prime } )$ for some other point $y ^ { \prime } \in Y$ . Since $Y$ is transitive, we have $y = g y ^ { \prime }$ for some $g \in U$ , and so $F = g F ^ { \prime }$ . We thus see that $F ^ { \prime }$ is isomorphic to the conjugate set $F ^ { g }$ , and so $\mu ( F ) = \mu ( F ^ { \prime } )$ by (3.1a) and (3.1d). Thus the condition in (3.1e) is independent of the choice of fiber. The slogan for (3.1e) is “ $\mu$ is multiplicative in fibrations.”

(b) If $X$ and $Y$ are finitary $\hat { G }$ -sets then $\mu ( X \times Y ) = \mu ( X ) \cdot \mu ( Y )$ . Indeed, by (3.1c), it suffices to treat the case where $X$ and $Y$ are transitive $U$ -sets, for some open subgroup $U$ , and then the identity follows from (3.1e) by considering the projection $X \times Y  Y$ .

(c) Let $U$ be an open subgroup of $G$ . Then a $\hat { U }$ -set is the same thing as a $\hat { G }$ -set. One easily sees that a measure for $G$ is also a measure for $U$ ; in other words, we can restrict measures from $G$ to $U$ . A measure for $U$ may not be a measure for $G$ , however, as conditions (d) and (e) are potentially stronger for $G$ than for $U$ .

(d) There is a relative notion of measure: given a stabilizer class $\mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { O } }$ , a measure for $( G , \mathcal { E } )$ assigns a value $\mu ( X )$ to each finitary $\mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { O } }$ -smooth $\hat { G }$ -set $X$ such that (a)–(e) hold when they make sense.

(e) Let $\mu$ be a $k$ -valued measure for $G$ , let $f \colon k  k ^ { \prime }$ be a ring homomorphism, and define $\mu ^ { \prime }$ by $\mu ^ { \prime } ( X ) = f ( \mu ( X ) )$ . Then $\mu ^ { \prime }$ is easily seen to be a measure. We refer to this construction as extension of scalars for measures. 

text: Example 3.3. Suppose $G$ is finite. Then any finitary $\hat { G }$ -set is finite, and we obtain a measure $\mu$ by defining $\mu ( X ) = \# X$ . In fact, this is the only measure: indeed, if $X$ is a finitary $\hat { G }$ -set then it is a finite disjoint union of singletons, and so its measure must by $\# X$ by (3.1b) and (3.1c). 

3.3. The ring $\Theta ( G )$ . Understanding the measures for $G$ is not a simple matter. To aid us in this task, we introduce the following ring:

Definition 3.6. We define a commutative ring $\Theta ( G )$ as follows. For each finitary $\hat { G }$ -set $X$ , there is an element $[ X ]$ of $\Theta ( G )$ . These elements are subject to the following relations (in which $X$ and $Y$ denote finitary $\hat { G }$ -sets):

list_items: (a) If $X$ and $Y$ are isomorphic then $[ X ] = [ Y ]$ .
(b) If $X$ is a singleton set then $[ X ] = 1$ .
(c) We have $\lfloor X \operatorname { I I } Y \rfloor = \lfloor X \rfloor + \lfloor Y \rfloor$ .
(d) For $g \in G$ we have $| X | = | X ^ { g } |$ , where $X ^ { g }$ is the conjugate of $X$ by $g$
(e) If $X$ and $Y$ are transitive $U$ -sets, for some open subgroup $U$ , and $X  Y$ is a map of $U$ -sets with fiber $F$ (over some point of $Y$ ), then $[ X ] = [ F ] \cdot [ Y ]$ .

text: More formally, $\Theta ( G )$ can be defined by taking the polynomial ring in variables indexed by isomorphism classes of finitary $\hat { G }$ -sets and forming the quotient by the ideal generated by relations corresponding to (b)–(e). 

If $\mu$ is a $k$ -valued measure for $G$ then we obtain a homomorphism $\Theta ( G ) \to k$ by $[ X ] \mapsto$ $\mu ( X )$ . Conversely, any homomorphism $\Theta ( G ) \to k$ yields a measure for $G$ . We thus see that there is a universal measure $\mu _ { \mathrm { u n i v } }$ for $G$ with values in $\Theta ( G )$ given by $\mu _ { \mathrm { u n i v } } ( X ) = [ X ]$ . In this way, understanding measures for $G$ is equivalent to understanding the ring $\Theta ( G )$ .
Remark 3.7. If $X$ and $Y$ are finitary $\hat { G }$ -sets then $[ X \times Y ] = [ X ] [ Y ]$ holds in $\Theta ( G )$ . This follows since $X \mapsto \lfloor X \rfloor$ is a measure. 

3.4. Basic properties of $\Theta ( G )$ . We now discuss some basic properties of $\Theta$ .

list_items: (a) Functorial behavior. If $U$ is an open subgroup of $G$ then there is a surjective ring homomorphism $\Theta ( U ) \to \Theta ( G )$ given by $[ X ] \mapsto [ X ]$ , for $X$ a finitary $\hat { U }$ -set. If $f \colon G \to H$ is a continuous surjection of pro-oligomorphic groups then there is a ring homomorphism $\Theta ( H ) \to \Theta ( G )$ given by $[ X ] \mapsto [ f ^ { * } ( X ) ]$ , where $X$ is a $\hat { H }$ -set and $f ^ { * } ( X )$ denotes the $\hat { G }$ -set obtained by letting $\hat { G }$ act through $f$ . If $\mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { o } } \subset \mathcal { F }$ are stabilizer classes, then there is a ring homomorphism $\Theta ( G ; { \mathcal { E } } ) \to \Theta ( G ; { \mathcal { F } } )$ given by $[ X ] \mapsto [ X ]$ . These statements all follow easily from the definitions.

(b) Finite sets. If $X$ is a $\hat { G }$ -set with $n < \infty$ elements then $X$ is isomorphic, as a $\hat { G }$ -set, to a disjoint union of $n$ one-point sets, and so $[ X ] = n$ in $\Theta ( G )$ . As a consequence, we see that $\Theta ( G ) = \mathbf { Z }$ if $G$ is a finite (or profinite) group. Indeed, the above discussion shows that the canonical map $\mathbf { Z } \to \Theta ( G )$ is surjective, while we also have a homomorphism $\Theta ( G ) \to \mathbf { Z }$ given by $[ X ] \mapsto \# X$ (see Example 3.3).
(c) Products. If $G$ and $H$ are pro-oligomorphic groups then there is a natural ring homomorphism

text:
$$
\Theta (G) \otimes \Theta (H) \to \Theta (G \times H), \qquad [ X ] \otimes [ Y ] \mapsto [ X \times Y ].

Indeed, this is just the product of the two pull-back maps from (a). This homomorphism may not be an isomorphism, though we know no counterexample. 3.5. The Burnside ring. The ring $\Theta ( G )$ is extremely subtle. It is closely related to a much more straightforward ring, the Burnside ring of $\hat { G }$ , which we now introduce. It is often convenient to use the Burnside ring as a starting point when studying $\Theta ( G )$ .

The Burnside ring of $G$ , denoted $\Omega ( G )$ , is the free abelian group on the set of isomorphism classes of transitive $G$ -sets. Given a transitive $G$ -set $X$ , we write $\mathbb { I } X \mathbb { I }$ for the corresponding basis vector of $\Omega ( G )$ . The unit element is the class J1K of the one-point set 1.

3.7. Regular measures. We now isolate two classes of measures that will play an important role, especially in Part III:

Definition 3.18. Let $\mu$ be a $k$ -valued measure for $G$ . We say that $\mu$ is regular if $\mu ( X )$ is a unit of $k$ for every transitive $G$ -set $X$ . We say that $\mu$ is quasi-regular if there is an open subgroup $U$ of $G$ such that $\mu | _ { U }$ is regular. 

Example 3.19. Suppose that $G$ is a finite group and $k$ is a field, and let $\mu$ be the unique measure for $G$ with values in $k$ (see Example 3.3). Then $\mu$ is regular if and only if $\# G$ is non-zero in $k$ . Thus, in the terminology of representation theory, “regular” coincides with the ordinary case, and “non-regular” with the modular case. For a general pro-oligomorphic group, it is reasonable to also consider regular as corresponding to the “ordinary case.” For instance, we prove an analog of Maschke’s theorem in this setting (Theorem 13.2). The measure $\mu$ is always quasi-regular: its restriction to the trivial subgroup is regular. 
It is clear that regular implies quasi-regular, and that both classes of measures are stable under extension of scalars. They are also stable under restricting to open subgroups:
Proposition 3.20. Let $\mu$ be a (quasi-)regular measure for $G$ . Then the restriction of $\mu$ to any open subgroup is again (quasi-)regular.

Proof. Suppose $\mu$ is regular and let $U$ be an open subgroup of $G$ . We show that $\mu | _ { U }$ is regular. Thus let $X$ be a transitive $U$ -set; we must show that $\mu ( X )$ is a unit of $k$ . Write $X = U / V$ for some open subgroup $V$ of $U$ . We have a fibration $G / U \to G / V$ with fiber $U / V$ , and so by (3.1e), $\mu ( G / U ) = \mu ( G / V ) \mu ( U / V )$ . Since $\mu ( G / U )$ and $\mu ( G / V )$ are units of $k$ , it follows that $\mu ( U / V )$ is as well.

Now suppose that $\mu$ is quasi-regular and let $U$ be an open subgroup of $G$ . We show that $\mu | _ { U }$ is quasi-regular. By definition, there is an open subgroup $V$ of $G$ such that $\mu | _ { V }$ is regular. By the previous paragraph, $\mu | _ { V \cap U }$ is regular. This shows that $\mu | _ { U }$ is quasi-regular, as required. 

Define $\Theta ^ { * } ( G )$ to be the localization of $\Theta ( G )$ obtained by inverting the classes $[ X ]$ for all transitive $G$ -sets $X$ . This ring classifies regular measures: a $k$ -valued regular measure is exactly a homomorphism $\Theta ^ { * } ( G ) \to k$ . If $U$ is an open subgroup of $G$ then a regular measure for $G$ restricts to a regular measure for $U$ (Proposition 3.20), and so the natural map $\Theta ( U ) \to \Theta ( G )$ induces a map $\Theta ^ { * } ( U ) \to \Theta ^ { * } ( G )$ .

3.8. Generalized index. To close §3, we give a more group-theoretic interpretation of measures. This perspective is not used in the remainder of the paper, but we have found it to be helpful to our own understanding. The following is the key concept:

Definition 3.24. A generalized index on $G$ with values in a commutative ring $k$ is a rule that assigns to every containment of open subgroups $V \subset U$ an element $\mathbb { U } : V \mathbb { I }$ of $k$ such that the following conditions hold:

list_items: (a) We have $\mathbb { U } : U \mathbb { I } = 1$ for all $U$ .
(b) We have $[ [ U : V ] ] = [ [ g U g ^ { - 1 } : g V g ^ { - 1 } ] ] $ for all $g \in G$
(c) Given open subgroups $W \subset V \subset U$ , we have $\lVert U : W \rVert = \lVert U : V \rVert \lVert V : W \rVert$ .
(d) Let $V , W \subset U$ be open subgroups of $G$ . Write $\textstyle U = \bigsqcup _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } V x _ { i } W$ . Then

text:
$$
\llbracket U: W \rrbracket = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \llbracket V: V \cap x _ {i} W x _ {i} ^ {- 1} \rrbracket .
$$
See Example 3.26 for an explanation of this identity.
The following proposition relates generalized indices to measures. We omit the proof since it is not used in the remainder of the paper; see [HS1, §3.6] for details.

Proposition 3.25. There is a bijection between generalized indices on $G$ with values in $k$ and measures on $G$ with values in $k$ , where the generalized index $[ [ - : - ] ]$ corresponds to the measure $\mu$ if $\mathbb { U } : V \mathbb { I } = \mu ( U / V )$ for all open subgroups $V \subset U$ .

Example 3.26. Suppose $G$ is finite. For subgroups $V \subset U$ , define $\mathbb { U } : V \mathbb { I }$ to be the usual index $\left[ U : V \right]$ . We claim that this is a generalized index. The first three conditions are clear, while the fourth follows from the decomposition

$$
U / W \cong \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} V / (V \cap x _ {i} W x _ {i} ^ {- 1}).
$$
Of course, this generalized index corresponds to the measure from Example 3.3.

Example 3.27. Recall that for $t \in \mathbf { C }$ there is an associated C-valued measure $\mu _ { t }$ for the infinite symmetric group $\mathfrak { S }$ (Example 3.4). By the above proposition, we can translate $\mu _ { t }$ into a $\mathbf { C }$ -valued generalized index $[ [ - : - ] ] _ { t }$ on $\mathfrak { S }$ . This generalized index satisfies

$$
\llbracket \mathfrak {S}: \mathfrak {S} (n) \rrbracket_ {t} = t (t - 1) \dots (t - n + 1), \qquad \llbracket \mathfrak {S}: \mathfrak {S} _ {n} \times \mathfrak {S} (n) \rrbracket_ {t} = \binom {t} {n}.
$$

Here ${ \mathfrak { S } } ( n )$ is the subgroup of $\mathfrak { S }$ fixing each of $1 , \ldots , n$ . Since the $\mu _ { t }$ account for all $\mathbf { C }$ -valued measures on $\mathfrak { S }$ , the proposition implies that generalized indices $\mathbb { I } - : - \mathbb { I } _ { t }$ account for all $\mathbf { C }$ -valued generalized indices on $\mathfrak { S }$ . 
