4. Integration

list_items: 4.1. Overview. Fix a pro-oligomorphic group $G$ , a ring $k$ , and a $k$ -valued measure $\mu$ for the duration of §4. The purpose of §4 is to introduce a theory of integration for oligomorphic groups. Precisely, for a $\hat { G }$ -set $X$ , we introduce the class of Schwartz functions on $X$ , and define an integral for them. We also define a push-forward operation on Schwartz functions with respect to a map $f \colon X \to Y$ of $\hat { G }$ -sets, and show that it has the expected properties. This theory of integration underlies the tensor category constructions later in the paper.

4.2. Schwartz functions. Let $X$ be a $\hat { G }$ -set and let $\varphi \colon X \to k$ be a function. We say that $\varphi$ is smooth if there is some group of definition $U$ for $X$ such that $\varphi$ is left $U$ -invariant, meaning $\varphi ( g x ) = \varphi ( x )$ for all $g \in U$ and $x \in X$ . We define the support of $\varphi$ to be the subset of $X$ where $\varphi$ is non-zero. If $\varphi$ is smooth then the support of $\varphi$ is a $\hat { G }$ -subset. In this case, we say that $\varphi$ has finitary support if its support is a finitary $\hat { G }$ -set. We say that $\varphi$ is a Schwartz function if it is smooth and has finitary support. We let ${ \mathcal { C } } ( X )$ be the set of Schwartz functions, which is naturally a $k$ -module. It is an analog of Schwartz space.

text: Let $A$ be a finitary $\hat { G }$ -subset of $X$ , and let $1 _ { A }$ be its indicator function. One easily sees that $1 _ { A }$ is a Schwartz function. We refer to a function of this form as elementary.
Proposition 4.1. The elementary functions generate ${ \mathcal { C } } ( X )$ as a $k$ -module.

Proof. Let $\varphi \in \mathcal { C } ( X )$ be given. Let $A$ be the support of $\varphi$ and let $U$ be a group of definition for $X$ such that $\varphi$ is $U$ -invariant; thus $A$ is $U$ -stable. Since $A$ is finitary, $U$ has finitely many orbits on $Y$ , say $A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n }$ . Since $\varphi$ is $U$ -invariant, it is constant on each orbit; let $c _ { i }$ be the common value of $\varphi$ on $A _ { i }$ . Then $\textstyle \varphi = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } c _ { i } \cdot 1 _ { A _ { i } }$ , which completes the proof. 

Remark 4.2. In fact, a more precise statement is true. Given any group of definition $U$ of $X$ , the functions $1 _ { A }$ with $A$ an orbit of an open subgroup of $U$ generate ${ \mathcal { C } } ( X )$ . This can be deduced easily from the proposition. 

Remark 4.3. The terminology “Schwartz function” is motivated by Bruhat’s generalization of the concept of Schwartz function to general locally compact abelian groups [Bru]: in the case of $\mathbf { Q } _ { p }$ , a (Bruhat-)Schwartz function is one that is smooth (locally constant) and compactly supported. 

4.3. Integration. Let $X$ be a $\hat { G }$ -set and let $\varphi \colon X \to k$ be a Schwartz function. Let $A$ b e the support of $\varphi$ , write $A = A _ { 1 } \sqcup \cdots \sqcup A _ { n }$ where the $A _ { i }$ are $\hat { G }$ -stable and $\varphi$ is constant on $A _ { i }$ , and let $c _ { i }$ be the common value of $f$ on $A _ { i }$ . We define the integral of $\varphi$ by

$$
\int_ {X} \varphi (x) d x = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} c _ {i} \mu (A _ {i}).
$$
It is a standard fact that this is well-defined: one can integrate finite sums of step functions against a finitely additive measure. A detailed proof is given in [HS1, §3.3].
It is clear that integration is $k$ -linear in the integrand $\varphi$ . Moreover, it is $G$ -equivariant, that is, we have

$$
\int_ {X ^ {g}} \varphi^ {g} (x) d x = \int_ {X} \varphi (x) d x,
$$
OLIGOMORPHIC GROUPS AND TENSOR CATEGORIES
where $g \in G$ and $X ^ { g }$ and $\varphi ^ { g }$ denote the conjugates by $g$ . Concretely, this allows us to make familiar changes of variables, e.g., if $X$ is a $G$ -set then we have

$$
\int_ {X} \varphi (x) d x = \int_ {X} \varphi (g x) d x
$$
for any $g \in G$ .
Example 4.4. Let $G$ be a finite group and let $X$ be a finitary $\hat { G }$ -set. Then $X$ is finite, and any function on $X$ is a Schwartz function. For $\varphi \in \mathcal { C } ( X )$ we have

$$
\int_ {X} \varphi (x) d x = \sum_ {x \in X} \varphi (x).
$$
Here we are integrating with respect to the unique measure for $G$ ; see Example 3.3. 

Example 4.5. Let $\mu$ be the measure $\mu _ { t }$ for the symmetric group $\mathfrak { S }$ described in Example 3.4. Suppose that $\varphi \in \mathcal { C } ( \Omega )$ . The smoothness condition exactly means that there is some integer $n \geq 0$ such that $\varphi ( m )$ is constant for $m > n$ ; let $c$ be this common value. Then

$$
\int_ {\Omega} \varphi (x) d x = c \cdot (t - n) + \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {n} \varphi (m).
$$
Note that the right side is indeed independent of the choice of $n$ .

Now suppose $\varphi \in \mathcal { C } ( \Omega ^ { 2 } )$ . We describe the basic procedure for computing its integral. First, $\Omega ^ { 2 }$ decomposes as the disjoint union of $\Omega ^ { [ 2 ] }$ and the diagonal, and the integral similarly decomposes. The diagonal is isomorphic to $\Omega$ and thus handled like the previous case, so we concentrate on the $\Omega ^ { [ 2 ] }$ integral. The smoothness condition implies that there is some integer $n \geq 0$ such that $\varphi ( i , j )$ is constant, say equal to $c$ , for all distinct $i , j > n$ . The integral over the $i , j > n$ region is equal to $2 c \cdot \binom { t - n } { 2 }$ . The remaining region decomposes into finitely many pieces which are either isomorphic to a cofinite subset of $\Omega$ (and can be handled as above) or singletons. Figure 1 depicts an example of what the level sets of $\varphi$ could look like. 

Example 4.6. Let ${ \cal G } = \mathrm { A u t } ( { \bf R } , < )$ and let $X$ be a finitary $\hat { G }$ -set. As we said in Example 3.5, $X$ is canonically a smooth manifold. A Schwartz functions on $X$ is constructible, i.e., its level sets are constructible sets. Our notion of integration (with respect to the measure from Example 3.5) is exactly integration with respect to Euler characteristic, as defined by Schapira and Viro (see, e.g., [Vir]). 

4.4. Push-forwards. We now show that there is a good theory of push-forward for Schwartz functions. We note that so far we have not made use of axiom (3.1e), but it will play a critical role in establishing basic properties of push-forward.
Let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a map of $\hat { G }$ -sets and let $\varphi \in \mathcal { C } ( X )$ . We define the push-forward $f _ { * } ( \varphi )$ to be the function on $Y$ given by

$$
(f _ {*} \varphi) (y) = \int_ {f ^ {- 1} (y)} \varphi (x) d x.
$$

Note that $f ^ { - 1 } ( y )$ is a $\hat { G }$ -subset of $X$ and the restriction of $\varphi$ to this set is a Schwartz function, and so the integral is defined. We now establish the basic properties of this construction.
Proposition 4.7. Push-forward preserves Schwartz space.
NATE HARMAN AND ANDREW SNOWDEN

Proof. Let $f$ and $\varphi$ be as above. Let $U$ be an open subgroup of $G$ such that (i) $U$ is a group of definition of $X$ and $Y$ ; (ii) $f$ is $U$ -equivariant; and (iii) $\varphi$ is left $U$ -invariant. Then for $g \in U$ and $y \in Y$ , we have

$$
(f _ {*} \varphi) (g y) = \int_ {f ^ {- 1} (g y)} \varphi (x) d x = \int_ {f ^ {- 1} (y)} \varphi (g ^ {- 1} x) d x = (f _ {*} \varphi) (x).
$$

where in the second step we used $f ^ { - 1 } ( g y ) = g f ^ { - 1 } ( y )$ and made the change of variables $x  g x$ , and in the third step we used the left $U$ -invariance of $\varphi$ . We thus see that $f _ { \ast } \varphi$ is left $U$ -invariant, and thus smooth. It is clear that the support of $f _ { \ast } \varphi$ is contained in the image of the support of $\varphi$ , and is therefore finitary. Thus $f _ { \ast } \varphi$ is a Schwartz function. 

We thus see that push-forward defines a $k$ -linear map $f _ { * } \colon { \mathcal { C } } ( X ) \to { \mathcal { C } } ( Y )$ . Note that if $Y = \mathbf { 1 }$ is a single point then we can identify ${ \mathcal { C } } ( Y )$ with $k$ , and $f _ { * }$ just becomes integration over $X$ .
Proposition 4.8 (Transitivity of push-forward). Let $f \colon X \to Y$ and $g \colon Y \to Z$ be maps of $\hat { G }$ -sets. Then $( g f ) _ { * } = g _ { * } f _ { * }$ .

Proof. Let $U$ be a group of definition for $X$ , $Y$ , and $Z$ such that $f$ and $g$ are $U$ -equivariant. Let $A$ be a $U$ -orbit $X$ , let $B = f ( A )$ , and let $C = g ( B )$ . Since $B$ is $U$ -transitive, all fibers of $f \colon A  B$ are $U$ -conjugate, and thus have the same measure; call it $a$ . Similarly define $b$ for $g \colon B \to C$ and $c$ for $g f \colon A  C$ . Computing directly, we find

We claim that $c = a b$ . Let $x \in A$ , let $V _ { 1 }$ be the stabilizer of $x$ , $V _ { 2 }$ the stabilizer of $f ( x )$ , and $V _ { 3 }$ the stabilizer of $g ( f ( x ) )$ . Thus $A \cong U / V _ { 1 }$ , $B \cong U / V _ { 2 }$ , and $C \cong U / V _ { 3 }$ . The fiber of $f \colon A  B$ is $V _ { 2 } / V _ { 1 }$ , and so $a = \mu ( V _ { 2 } / V _ { 1 } )$ . The fiber of $g \colon B \to C$ is $V _ { 3 } / V _ { 2 }$ , and so $b =$ $\mu ( V _ { 3 } / V _ { 2 } )$ . The fiber of $g f \colon A  C$ is $V _ { 3 } / V _ { 1 }$ , and so $c = \mu ( V _ { 3 } / V _ { 1 } )$ . We must therefore show $\mu ( V _ { 3 } / V _ { 1 } ) = \mu ( V _ { 2 } / V _ { 1 } ) \mu ( V _ { 3 } / V _ { 2 } )$ . This follows from (3.1e), as the natural map $V _ { 3 } / V _ { 1 } \to V _ { 3 } / V _ { 2 }$ has fiber $V _ { 2 } / V _ { 1 }$ . This establishes the claim. We thus have $( g f ) _ { * } ( 1 _ { A } ) = g _ { * } ( f _ { * } ( 1 _ { A } ) )$ . Since the functions $1 _ { A }$ span ${ \mathcal { C } } ( X )$ by Remark 4.2, the result follows. 
Corollary 4.9 (Fubini’s theorem). Let $X$ and $Y$ be $\hat { G }$ -sets and let $\varphi \in \mathcal { C } ( X \times Y )$ . Then

$$
\int_ {X \times Y} \varphi (x, y) d (x, y) = \int_ {X} \int_ {Y} \varphi (x, y) d y d x.
$$

Proof. Let $p \colon X \times Y \to Y$ be the projection map and let $f \colon X \times Y  { \mathbf { 1 } }$ and $g \colon Y  { \mathbf { 1 } }$ b e the unique maps. Then $f = g \circ p$ , and so $f _ { * } = g _ { * } \circ p _ { * }$ by Proposition 4.8. This exactly gives the stated formula. 

Corollary 4.10. Let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a map of finitary $\hat { G }$ -sets such that each fiber is finite of cardinality $n$ . Then $\mu ( X ) = n \cdot \mu ( Y )$ , and $[ X ] = n \cdot [ Y ]$ in $\Theta ( G )$ .

Proof. We have $f _ { * } ( 1 _ { X } ) = n \cdot 1 _ { Y }$ . Applying push-forward along $Y  { \bf 1 }$ yields the first formula. The second follows by considering the universal measure valued in $\Theta ( G )$ . 

Given a map $f \colon X \to Y$ of $\hat { G }$ -sets and a function $\psi \colon Y  k$ on $Y$ , we let $f ^ { * } ( \psi )$ be the function on $X$ given by $( f ^ { * } \psi ) ( x ) = \psi ( f ( x ) )$ . If $\psi$ is smooth then so is $f ^ { * } ( \psi )$ . However, $f ^ { * }$ does not preserve Schwartz space in general. It does if $X$ is finitary, as then any smooth function is a Schwartz function.
OLIGOMORPHIC GROUPS AND TENSOR CATEGORIES

Proposition 4.11 (Projection formula). Let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a map of $\hat { G }$ -sets, let $\varphi \in \mathcal { C } ( X )$ , and let $\psi \in \mathcal { C } ( Y )$ . Then $f ^ { * } ( \psi ) \varphi$ is a Schwartz function on $X$ and $f _ { * } ( f ^ { * } ( \psi ) \varphi ) = \psi f _ { * } ( \varphi )$ .
Proof. The function $f ^ { * } ( \psi ) \varphi$ is smooth, and its support is contained in the support of $\varphi$ , and thus finitary; hence it is Schwartz. We have

$$
f _ {*} (f ^ {*} (\psi) \varphi) (y) = \int_ {f ^ {- 1} (y)} (f ^ {*} \psi) (x) \varphi (x) d x = \psi (y) \int_ {f ^ {- 1} (y)} \varphi (x) d x = \psi (y) (f _ {*} \varphi) (y),
$$
where in the second step we used that $( f ^ { * } \psi ) ( x ) = \psi ( y )$ is constant and thus pulls out of the integral. 
Proposition 4.12 (Base change). Consider a cartesian square of finitary $\hat { G }$ -sets
Then for $\varphi \in \mathcal { C } ( X )$ we have

$$
g ^ {*} (f _ {*} \varphi) = f _ {*} ^ {\prime} ((g ^ {\prime}) ^ {*} \varphi).
$$
Proof. Put $\psi _ { 1 } = g ^ { * } ( f _ { * } \varphi )$ and $\psi _ { 2 } = f _ { * } ^ { \prime } ( ( g ^ { \prime } ) ^ { * } \varphi )$ . Let $y ^ { \prime } \in Y ^ { \prime }$ . Then

$$
\psi_ {1} (y ^ {\prime}) = \int_ {f ^ {- 1} \left(g \left(y ^ {\prime}\right)\right)} \varphi (x) d x
$$

The map $g ^ { \prime } \colon ( f ^ { \prime } ) ^ { - 1 } ( y ^ { \prime } ) \to f ^ { - 1 } ( g ( y ^ { \prime } ) )$ is an isomorphism of $\hat { G }$ -sets. Thus the two integrals above are equal, and so $\psi _ { 1 } = \psi _ { 2 }$ . 
5. The $\Theta$ ring is binomial

5.1. The main theorem. Fix a pro-oligomorphic group $G$ for the duration of §5. Recall that a commutative ring $R$ is called a binomial ring if it is torsion free as a $\mathbf { Z }$ -module and for every $x \in R$ and $n \in \mathbf N$ , the element
of $R \otimes \mathbf { Q }$ belongs to $R$ . The purpose of §5 is to prove the following theorem:
Theorem 5.1. The ring $\Theta ( G )$ is a binomial ring.
The theorem has some strong ramifications concerning measures:

Corollary 5.2. Let $\mu$ be a measure for $G$ with values in a field $k$ of characteristic $p > 0$ . Then µ takes values in the prime subfield $\mathbf { F } _ { p } \subset k$ , and lifts uniquely to a $\mathbf { Z } _ { p }$ -valued measure.

Proof. Regard $\mu$ as a ring homomorphism $\Theta ( G ) \to k$ . For any binomial ring $R$ , one has $x ^ { p } = x$ for $x \in R / p R$ [Eli, Theorem 4.1], and so any homomorphism $R \to k$ lands in $\mathbf { F } _ { p }$ . The lifting statement follows from the discussion in [Eli, §9]. 
Corollary 5.3. If an oligomorphic group admits any measure then it admits a C-valued measure.
NATE HARMAN AND ANDREW SNOWDEN

Proof. Let $G$ be oligomorphic, and suppose that $G$ admits some measure. Then $\Theta ( G )$ is non-zero. Since $\Theta ( G )$ is torsion-free (Theorem 5.1) it follows that $\Theta ( G ) \otimes \mathbf { Q }$ is non-zero. Since $\Theta ( G )$ is countable (§3.4(f)) the result follows from the fact that any non-zero countable Q-algebra admits a homomorphism to $\mathbf { C }$ . 
Corollary 5.4. If $\Theta ( G )$ is finitely generated as a ring then there is a ring isomorphism

$$
\Theta (G) \cong \mathbf {Z} [ 1 / m _ {1} ] \times \dots \times \mathbf {Z} [ 1 / m _ {r} ]
$$
for some $r \geq 0$ and integers $m _ { 1 } , \ldots , m _ { r }$
Proof. This is a general result for finitely generated binomial rings [Xan, Theorem 9]. 

Remark 5.5. There are many examples where $\Theta ( G ) \otimes \mathbf { Q }$ is finitely generated as a Q-algebra and of positive Krull dimension. In these cases, the above corollary implies that $\Theta ( G )$ cannot be finitely generated. For instance, this happens when $G$ is the infinite symmetric group: here, $\Theta ( G )$ is the ring of integer-valued polynomials, which is not finitely generated, but $\Theta ( G ) \otimes \mathbf { Q } \cong \mathbf { Q } [ t ]$ . The situation in the corollary occurs for the group $\mathrm { A u t } ( { \bf R } , < )$ and the group attached to boron trees. 

To prove the theorem, we show that $\Theta ( G )$ carries the structure of a $\lambda$ -ring, with $\lambda ^ { n } ( [ X ] ) =$ $\big [ X ^ { ( n ) } \big ]$ . We then show that the Adam’s operations are trivial. A theorem of Elliott states that any such $\lambda$ -ring is binomial, and so this yields the theorem.

Remark 5.6. Let $X$ be a finitary $\hat { G }$ -set and let $x = [ X ]$ be its class in $\Theta ( G )$ . It is easy to see that $[ X ^ { | n | } ] = x ( x - 1 ) \cdots ( x - n + 1 )$ . Moreover, the natural map $X ^ { [ n ] } \to X ^ { ( n ) }$ is $n !$ !-to-1, and so $[ X ^ { [ n ] } ] = n ! \cdot [ X ^ { ( n ) } ]$ by Corollary 4.10. Thus if we knew that $\Theta ( G )$ were torsion-free then we would have ${ \binom { x } { n } } = [ X ^ { ( n ) } ]$ , and so $\Theta ( G )$ would be a binomial ring. Thus, in a sense, the real content of Theorem 5.1 is the torsion-freeness. However, we do not know how to prove this directly. Instead, as stated above, we construct operations like $x \mapsto { \binom { x } { n } }$ on $\Theta ( G )$ , and then deduce the theorem from properties of these operations. 
Remark 5.7. There is a relative version of Theorem 5.1. Let $\mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { O } }$ be a stabilizer class satisfying the following condition:
(∗) If $X$ is an $\mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { O } }$ -smooth $G$ -set then so is $X ^ { ( n ) }$ , for any $n \geq 0$

Then $\Theta ( G ; \mathcal { E } )$ is a binomial ring. This follows from the proof of Theorem 5.1. If $\mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { O } }$ does not satisfy (∗) then $\Theta ( G ; \mathcal { E } )$ need not be a binomial ring: for example, when $G$ is the infinite symmetric group and $\mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { O } }$ is the stabilizer class from Example 2.11, we find that $\Theta ( G ; { \mathcal { E } } ) = \mathbf { Z } [ x ]$ (Proposition 14.15), which is not a binomial ring. We do not know if $\Theta ( G ; \mathcal { E } )$ is always torsion-free. 

5.2. $\lambda$ -rings. We now recall the basic definitions surrounding $\lambda$ -rings. We refer to [Die, §3] or [Knu, §I] for additional details. We note that some sources (such as [Knu]) use the terminology “pre- $\lambda$ -ring” and “ $\lambda$ -ring” in place of our “ $\lambda$ -ring” and “special $\lambda$ -ring.”

Definition 5.8. A $\lambda$ -ring is a commutative ring $R$ equipped with (set) maps $\lambda ^ { n } \colon R  R$ for all non-negative integers $n$ such that the following conditions hold (for $x , y \in R$ ):

list_items: (b) $\lambda ^ { 1 } ( x ) = x$
(c) $\begin{array} { r } { \lambda ^ { n } ( x + y ) = \sum _ { i + j = n } \lambda ^ { i } ( x ) \lambda ^ { j } ( y ) } \end{array}$ for all $n \geq 0$

text: A $\lambda$ -ring is called special if the following additional conditions hold:

list_items: (d) $\lambda ^ { n } ( 1 ) = 0$ for $n \geq 2$ .
(e) $\lambda ^ { n } ( x y ) = P _ { n } ( \lambda ^ { 1 } ( x ) , \ldots , \lambda ^ { n } ( x ) , \lambda ^ { 1 } ( y ) , \ldots , \lambda ^ { n } ( y ) )$ for all $n \geq 0$
(f) $\lambda ^ { n } ( \lambda ^ { m } ( x ) ) = P _ { n , m } ( \lambda ^ { 1 } ( x ) , \ldots , \lambda ^ { n m } ( x ) )$ for all $n , m \geq 0$

text: Here $P _ { n }$ and $P _ { n , m }$ are certain universal polynomials; see [Die, §3.1] or [Knu, §I.1] for the precise definitions. 

Definition 5.9. Let $R$ and $S$ be $\lambda$ -rings. A homomorphism of $\lambda$ -rings is a ring homomorphism $f \colon R \to S$ such that $f ( \lambda ^ { i } ( x ) ) = \lambda ^ { i } ( f ( x ) )$ for all $x \in R$ and all $i \geq 0$ . 
Example 5.10. The ring $\mathbf { Z }$ of integers is a special $\lambda$ -ring via $\textstyle \lambda ^ { n } ( x ) \ = \ { \binom { x } { n } }$ . See [Knu, §I.2].

Example 5.11. The Burnside ring $\Omega ( G )$ carries a $\lambda$ -ring structure given by $\lambda ^ { n } ( \left[ X \right] ) =$ $\mathbb { [ } X ^ { ( n ) } ] ]$ . Conditions (a) and (b) are clear, while (c) follows from the natural isomorphism

$$
(X \operatorname {I I} Y) ^ {(n)} = \coprod_ {i + j = n} \left(X ^ {(i)} \times Y ^ {(j)}\right).
$$
This $\lambda$ -structure is typically not special, even when $G$ is finite; see [Sie].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Let $\Lambda ( R )$ be the set $1 + t R [ [ t ] ]$ of all formal power series with coefficients in $R$ having constant term 1. Let $a , b \in \Lambda ( R )$ , and write $\textstyle a = \sum _ { i \geq 0 } a _ { i } t ^ { \iota }$ and $\begin{array} { r } { b = \sum _ { i \geq 0 } b _ { i } t ^ { i } } \end{array}$ with $a _ { i } , b _ { i } \in R$ and $a _ { 0 } = b _ { 0 } = 1$ . We make the following definitions:

list_items: • $a \oplus b$ is the ordinary power series product $a b$ .
• $\begin{array} { r } { a \otimes b = \sum _ { n \geq 0 } P _ { n } ( a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n } , b _ { 1 } , \ldots , b _ { n } ) t ^ { n } } \end{array}$
• $\begin{array} { r } { \lambda ^ { i } ( a ) = \sum _ { n \geq 0 } P _ { n , i } ( a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n i } ) t ^ { n } } \end{array}$

text: Grothendieck proved that $\bigoplus$ and $\otimes$ give $\Lambda ( R )$ the structure of a commutative, associative, unital ring, and that the $\lambda ^ { i }$ define on it the structure of a special $\lambda$ -ring; see [Knu, §I.2] or [Die, Proposition 3.1.8]. (The multiplicative identity in $\Lambda ( R )$ is $1 + t$ .) This ring is sometimes called the ring of “big Witt vectors.” If $\varphi \colon R  S$ is a ring homomorphism, then there is an induced homomorphism of $\lambda$ -rings $\varphi \colon \Lambda ( R ) \to \Lambda ( S )$ , by $\begin{array} { r } { \varphi ( \sum _ { i \geq 0 } a _ { i } t ^ { i } ) = \sum _ { i \geq 0 } \varphi ( a _ { i } ) t ^ { i } } \end{array}$ .

Suppose now that we have functions $\lambda ^ { n } \colon R  R$ for all $n \geq 0$ , with $\lambda ^ { 0 } ( x ) = 1$ and $\lambda ^ { 1 } ( x ) = x$ for all $x$ . Define a function $\lambda _ { t } \colon R \to \Lambda ( R )$ by $\begin{array} { r } { \lambda _ { t } ( x ) = \sum _ { n \geq 0 } \lambda ^ { n } ( x ) t ^ { n } } \end{array}$ . Then the $\lambda ^ { n }$ define a $\lambda$ -ring structure on $R$ if and only if $\lambda _ { t }$ is an additive group homomorphism. Assuming this, the $\lambda ^ { n }$ define a special $\lambda$ -ring structure on $R$ if and only if $\lambda _ { t }$ is a homomorphism of $\lambda$ -rings.
Suppose that $R$ is a $\lambda$ -ring, and let $\lambda _ { t } \colon R \to \Lambda ( R )$ be as above. For $x \in R$ and $n \geq 1$ define $\psi ^ { n } ( x ) \in R$ by the identity

$$
\frac {d}{d t} \log \lambda_ {t} (x) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} (- 1) ^ {n} \psi^ {n + 1} (x) t ^ {n}.

Then $\psi ^ { n } \colon R \to R$ is called the $n$ th Adam’s operation associated to the $\lambda$ -ring structure. 6. The model-theoretic perspective

6.1. Overview. There is an intimate connection between oligomorphic groups and model theory. We review this in some detail in §6.2, but provide an abridged rendition here. Suppose $\mathfrak { A }$ is some class of finite structures, e.g., total orders, partial orders, graphs, etc. Under certain conditions, one can form the Fra¨ıss´e limit of the class $\mathfrak { A }$ ; this is a countable structure $\Omega$ that contains a copy of every member of $\mathfrak { A }$ and satisfies an important homogeneity property. In many cases, the automorphism group $G$ of $\Omega$ acts oligomorphically on $\Omega$ . In this way, Fra¨ıss´e limits provide a powerful way of constructing oligomorphic groups; in fact, most examples of oligomorphic groups are constructed via this procedure.

Suppose we have $\mathfrak { A }$ , $\Omega$ , and $G$ as above, and $G$ acts oligomorphically. Since $G$ is completely determined by $\mathfrak { A }$ , one can translate anything about $G$ to the model-theoretic side, at least in principle. The purpose of §6 is to perform this translation for the concept of measure. In Definition 6.2, we introduce the notion of measure for $\mathfrak { A }$ . The main result of this section, Theorem 6.9, establishes an equivalence between measures for $\mathfrak { A }$ and measures for $G$ .

In some cases it is extremely difficult to understand anything about $G$ directly, e.g., for the automorphism group of the universal boron tree or Rago graph. In these cases, the only way to effectively work with measures is through the dictionary established here. Even in cases where one can understand something about $G$ , the model-theoretic perspective can still provide substantial insight. We will see some examples of this as we go; for a more substantive example, see §17.

There is one other significant result in this section we wish to highlight: Theorem 6.24 gives a model-theoretic criterion for $\Theta$ to be non-zero. While we believe this is a significant step in understanding $\Theta$ , it does not apply very broadly. Expanding the scope of this theorem is an important problem.

6.2. Fra¨ıss´e’s theorem. We now provide some background on model theory and Fra¨ıss´e’s theorem. We refer to the book [Cam3] and the survery article [Mac] for more details.

6.2.1. Structures. A signature (of a first order relational language) is a collection $\Sigma =$ $\{ ( R _ { i } , n _ { i } ) \} _ { i \in I }$ where $R _ { i }$ is a symbol and $n _ { i }$ is a positive integer, called the arity of $R _ { i }$ . Fix a signature $\Sigma$ for the remainder of this section. A structure (for $\Sigma$ ) is a set $X$ equipped with, for each $i \in I$ , an $n _ { i }$ -arity relation $R _ { i }$ on $X$ (i.e., a subset of $X ^ { n _ { i } }$ ). There is an obvious notion of isomorphism of structures. If $X$ is a structure and $Y$ is a subset of $X$ , there is an induced structure on $Y$ : simply restrict each relation from $X$ to $Y$ . The structures obtained in this way are the substructures of $X$ . An embedding $i \colon Y \to X$ of structures is an injective function that induces an isomorphism between $Y$ and the substructure $i ( Y )$ .

6.2.2. Amalgamations. Let $i \colon Y \to X$ and $j \colon Y  Y ^ { \prime }$ be embeddings of structures. An amalgamation of $( i , j )$ is a triple $( X ^ { \prime } , i ^ { \prime } , j ^ { \prime } )$ consisting of a structure $X ^ { \prime }$ and embeddings $i ^ { \prime } \colon Y ^ { \prime } \to X ^ { \prime }$ and $j ^ { \prime } \colon X \to X ^ { \prime }$ such that two conditions hold:

list_items: (a) $i ^ { \prime }$ and $j ^ { \prime }$ agree on $Y$ , that is, $i ^ { \prime } \circ j = i \circ j ^ { \prime }$
(b) $i ^ { \prime }$ and $j ^ { \prime }$ are jointly surjective, that is, $X ^ { \prime } = \operatorname { i m } ( i ^ { \prime } ) \cup \operatorname { i m } ( j ^ { \prime } )$ .

text: Thus, intuitively, an amalgamation is obtained by glueing $X$ and $Y ^ { \prime }$ together along the common copy of $Y$ . Note that amalgamations can identify more than required, i.e., the intersections of (the images of) $X$ and $Y ^ { \prime }$ in $X ^ { \prime }$ can be larger than (the image of) $Y$ .

If $( X ^ { \prime \prime } , i ^ { \prime \prime } , j ^ { \prime \prime } )$ is a second amalgamation, an isomorphism of amalgamations is an isomorphism $k \colon X ^ { \prime } \to X ^ { \prime \prime }$ of structures such that $i ^ { \prime \prime } = k \circ i ^ { \prime }$ and $j ^ { \prime \prime } = k \circ j ^ { \prime }$ . Amalgamations have no non-trivial automorphisms: in effect, $X ^ { \prime }$ is labeled by $i ^ { \prime }$ and $j ^ { \prime }$ , and an automorphism must preserve the labeling. We often list “the” amalgamations of $( i , j )$ ; such lists are always intended to contain exactly one member from each isomorphism class.

6.2.3. Homogeneous structures. A structure $\Omega$ is homogeneous if the following condition holds: given finite substructures $X$ and $Y$ of $\Omega$ and an isomorphism $i \colon Y \ \to \ X$ , there exists an automorphism $\sigma$ of $\Omega$ extending $i$ (i.e., $\sigma ( y ) = i ( y )$ for all $y \in Y$ ). Suppose $\Omega$ is homogeneous and let $G$ be its automorphism group. Then two finite subsets of $\Omega$ , equipped with the induced substructures, are abstractly isomorphic if and only if they belong to the same $G$ -orbit. We thus see that the $G$ -orbits on $\Omega ^ { ( n ) }$ are in bijection with the isomorphism classes of $n$ -element substructures of $\Omega$ . In particular, if for each $n$ there are only finitely many isomorphism types of $n$ -element substructures of $\Omega$ then $G$ acts oligomorphically on $\Omega$ (and conversely). In this way, homogeneous structures provide a bridge between model theory and oligomorphic groups.

6.2.4. Ages. The age of a structure $\Omega$ , denoted $\mathrm { a g e } ( \Omega )$ , is the class of all finite structures that embed into $\Omega$ . Suppose $\Omega$ is a countable homogeneous structure, and put ${ \mathfrak { A } } = { \mathrm { a g e } } ( { \Omega } )$ . Then $\mathfrak { A }$ has the following properties:

list_items: (a) If $X \in { \mathfrak { A } }$ and $Y$ is isomorphic to $X$ then $Y \in { \mathfrak { A } }$
(b) If $X \in { \mathfrak { A } }$ and $Y$ is a substructure of $X$ then $Y \in { \mathfrak { A } }$ .
(c) Up to isomorphism, $\mathfrak { A }$ has only countably many members.

(d) Given embeddings $i \colon Y \to X$ and $j \colon Y \to Y ^ { \prime }$ , with $X , Y , Y ^ { \prime } \in { \mathfrak { A } }$ , there is an amalgamation $( X ^ { \prime } , i ^ { \prime } , j ^ { \prime } )$ of $( i , j )$ with $X ^ { \prime } \in { \mathfrak { A } }$ .

6.2.5. Fra¨ıss´e’s theorem. This extremely influential theorem was proven by Roland Fra¨ıss´e in the early 1950’s [Fra], and provides a converse to the discussion in §6.2.4:

Theorem 6.1. Let A be a class of finite structures satisfying (a)–(d) from §6.2.4. Then there is a countable homogeneous structure $\Omega$ such that ${ \mathfrak { A } } = { \mathrm { a g e } } ( { \Omega } )$ . Moreover, Ω is unique up to isomorphism.

A proof of Fra¨ıss´e’s theorem can be found in [Cam3, §2.6]. 6.2.6. Example: total orders. Let $\mathfrak { A }$ be the class of all finite totally ordered sets. (The signature in this case consists of a single binary relation.) This is easily seen to be a Fra¨ıss´e class. Thus $\mathfrak { A }$ is the age of a countable homogeneous structure $\Omega$ .

To see that $\mathbf { Q }$ is homogeneous, suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are finite subsets of $\mathbf { Q }$ and $i \colon Y \to X$ is an order-preserving bijection. Since $X$ and $Y$ have the same cardinality, we can thus find an order-preserving bijection $\sigma \colon \mathbf { Q }  \mathbf { Q }$ such that $\sigma ( Y ) = X$ ; in fact, we can take $\sigma$ to be a piecewise linear function. The restriction of $\sigma$ to $Y$ necessarily induces $i$ , as there is only one order-preserving bijection $Y  X$ . The uniqueness aspect of the Fra¨ıss´e limit, in this case, amounts to the fact that any two countable dense total orders are isomorphic, a statement first proved by Cantor.

Part II. Permutation representations
7. Matrix algebra

7.1. Overview. An $n \times m$ matrix with entries in a ring $k$ can be thought of as a function $[ n ] \times [ m ] \to k$ . If $Y$ and $X$ are finitary $\hat { G }$ -sets then, by analogy, we define a $Y \times X$ matrix to be a Schwartz function $Y \times X \to k$ . It turns out that many familiar ideas from linear algebra— including matrix multiplication, trace, determinant, and eigenvalues—can be adapted to this setting, if we have a measure.

The purpose of §7 is to develop these ideas. This theory will play a significant role in our work on the representation categories Perm(G) and Rep Rep(G). The most important result in §7 is Theorem 7.11, which shows that nilpotent matrices have vanishing trace (under a certain hypothesis). This result is used to show that certain endomorphism algebras in Perm(G) are semi-simple, which is an important step in the proof of Theorem 13.2.
We fix a pro-oligomorphic group $G$ and a $k$ -valued measure $\mu$ throughout §7.
7.2. Matrices and vectors. The following is the main concept studied in §7:
Definition 7.1. Let $X$ and $Y$ be finitary $\hat { G }$ -sets. A $Y \times X$ matrix $A$ with entries in $k$ is a Schwartz function $A \colon Y \times X \to k$ . 
NATE HARMAN AND ANDREW SNOWDEN

Of course, in a sense this definition does not introduce anything new: matrices are the same mathematical objects as Schwartz functions. However, having a different name and notation will be helpful psychologically and in providing context.
We now introduce a few more notations, conventions, and definitions:

list_items: • We write $\operatorname { M a t } _ { Y , X } ( k )$ , or simply $\operatorname { M a t } _ { Y , X }$ , for the set of all $Y \times X$ matrices. By convention, whenever we write $\operatorname { M a t } _ { Y , X }$ we mean that $X$ and $Y$ are finitary $\hat { G }$ -sets. We write $\operatorname { M a t } _ { X }$ in place of ${ \mathrm { M a t } } _ { X , X }$ .

• Suppose $U$ is a group of definition for $X$ and $Y$ . We say that a matrix $A \in \operatorname { M a t } _ { Y , X }$ is $U$ -invariant if $A ( g x , g y ) = A ( x , y )$ for all $g \in U$ , $x \in X$ , $y \in Y$ . We write $\mathrm { M a t } _ { Y , X } ^ { U }$ for the set of $U$ -invariant matrices. We note that $\operatorname { M a t } _ { Y , X } ^ { U }$ can be identified with the space of functions $U \backslash ( Y \times X )  k$ , and is thus a free $k$ -module of finite rank.

• We define the identity matrix $I _ { X } \in \mathrm { M a t } _ { X }$ by $I _ { X } ( x , y ) = 1 _ { \Delta } ( x , y )$ , where $\Delta \subset X \times X$ is the diagonal. We sometimes write 1 in place of $I _ { X }$ .

• For $A \in \operatorname { M a t } _ { Y , X }$ , we define the tranpose of $A$ , denoted $A ^ { t }$ , to be the element of ${ \mathrm { M a t } } _ { X , Y }$ given by $A ^ { t } ( x , y ) = A ( y , x )$ .

• We write $\operatorname { V e c } _ { X }$ in place of $\operatorname { M a t } _ { X , { \bf 1 } }$ . We think of $\operatorname { V e c } _ { X }$ as the space of column vectors of height $X$ . It is sometimes also helpful to think of elements of $\operatorname { V e c } _ { X }$ as infinite linear combinations of elements of $X$ . We note that $\operatorname { V e c } _ { X }$ is just another name for ${ \mathcal { C } } ( X )$ .

text: One of the most interesting features about matrices in classical linear algebra is matrix multiplication. We now extend this to our setting. Let $B \in \mathrm { M a t } _ { Y , X }$ and $A \in \mathrm { M a t } _ { Z , Y }$ . We define the product matrix $A B \in \operatorname { M a t } _ { Z , X }$ by

$$
(A B) (z, x) = \int_ {Y} A (z, y) B (y, x) d y.
$$

One can view $A B$ as the push-forward of the integrand appearing above along the projection map $Z \times Y \times X \to Z \times X$ , and so by general properties of push-forwards (specifically Proposition 4.7) it is indeed a Schwartz function on $Z \times X$ .
Proposition 7.2. Matrix multiplication is associative (when defined), and the identity matrix is the identity for multiplication (when defined).
Proof. Let $A$ and $B$ be as above, and let $C \in \mathrm { M a t } _ { X , W }$ . Then

where in the final step we used Fubini’s theorem (Corollary 4.9). By a similar computation, one sees that $( ( A B ) C ) ( z , w )$ is equal to the last line above as well, which proves associativity. Let $C \in \mathrm { M a t } _ { X , W }$ be as above. Then

$$
(I _ {X} \cdot C) (x, w) = \int_ {X} 1 _ {\Delta} (x, x ^ {\prime}) C (x ^ {\prime}, w) d x ^ {\prime} = C (x, w).
$$
Thus $I _ { X } \cdot C = C$ . A similar computation shows that $B \cdot I _ { X } = B$ for $B$ as above.
Corollary 7.3. Mat $X$ is an associative unital algebra under matrix multiplication.

Example 7.4. Consider the permutation representation ${ \bf C } ^ { n }$ of the symmetric group ${ \mathfrak { S } } _ { n }$ . Let $A _ { n } \colon { \mathbf { C } } ^ { n } \to { \mathbf { C } } ^ { n }$ be the map sending every basis vector to the invariant vector $\sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } e _ { i }$ . The matrix for $A _ { n }$ has every entry equal to 1. We have $A _ { n } ^ { 2 } = n A _ { n }$ . For $n \geq 2$ , the space $\operatorname { E n d } _ { \mathfrak { S } _ { n } } ( \mathbf { C } ^ { n } )$ is two-dimensional, with basis 1 and $A _ { n }$ .

Now consider the infinite symmetric group $\mathfrak { S }$ acting on $\Omega = \{ 1 , 2 , . . . \}$ , and let $\mu _ { t }$ be the measure from Example 3.4. Let $A \in \mathrm { M a t } _ { \Omega }$ be the constant function $A ( x , y ) = 1$ . Then, as above, $A ^ { 2 } = t A$ , and the matrices 1 and $A$ form a basis for $\mathrm { M a t } _ { \Omega } ^ { \mathfrak { S } }$ . One can view $A$ as a sort of limit of the $A _ { n }$ ’s. 

For $A \in \mathrm { M a t } _ { Y , X }$ and $v \in \mathrm { V e c } _ { X }$ , we can consider the matrix-vector product $A v \in \mathrm { V e c } _ { Y }$ ; this is defined simply by treating $\boldsymbol { v }$ as an $X \times \mathbf { 1 }$ matrix. This product defines a map

$$
A \colon \operatorname {V e c} _ {X} \to \operatorname {V e c} _ {Y}, \quad v \mapsto A v.
$$
As usual, this function determines the matrix $A$ :
Proposition 7.5. Let $A , B \in \operatorname { M a t } _ { Y , X }$ be two matrices such that $A v = B v$ for all $v \in \mathrm { V e c } _ { X }$ . Then $A = B$ .
Proof. Suppose $\boldsymbol { v }$ is the point mass at $x$ . Then

$$
(A v) (y) = \int_ {X} A (y, x ^ {\prime}) v (x ^ {\prime}) d x ^ {\prime} = A (y, x).
$$

We thus see that $A v$ is the “ $x$ th column” of $A$ . Thus the function $A \colon \operatorname { V e c } _ { X }  \operatorname { V e c } _ { Y }$ determines all the columns of $A$ , and thus $A$ itself. 
7.3. Traces. Let $A \in \operatorname { M a t } _ { X }$ . We define the trace of $A$ by

$$
\operatorname {t r} (A) = \int_ {X} A (x, x) d x.
$$
Trace has the usual symmetry property:
Proposition 7.6. Let $A \in \operatorname { M a t } _ { Y , X }$ and $B \in \operatorname { M a t } _ { X , Y }$ . Then $\operatorname { t r } ( A B ) = \operatorname { t r } ( B A )$ .
Proof. By definition,

$$
(A B) (y, y ^ {\prime}) = \int_ {X} A (y, x) B (x, y ^ {\prime}) d x,
$$
and so

$$
\operatorname {t r} (A B) = \int_ {Y} \int_ {X} A (y, x) B (x, y) d x d y = \int_ {X \times Y} A (y, x) B (x, y) d (x, y),
$$
where we used Fubini’s theorem (Corollary 4.9) in the second step. A similar manipulation leads to an identical expression for $\operatorname { t r } ( B A )$ . 

7.4. Trace of nilpotents. A fundamental property of nilpotent matrices, in classical linear algebra, is that they have vanishing trace. We now establish this for our matrices, under a hypothesis. This result will play an important role in proving semi-simplicity results later on (see Proposition 7.19). The following is the key observation:
Proposition 7.8. If $k$ is a field of positive characteristic $p$ and $A \in \operatorname { M a t } _ { X }$ then

$$
\operatorname {t r} (A) ^ {p} = \operatorname {t r} (A ^ {p}).
$$

Proof. By Corollary 5.2, the measure $\mu$ is valued in $\mathbf { F } _ { p }$ , and lifts uniquely to a measure $\tilde { \mu }$ valued in $\mathbf { Z } _ { p }$ . Suppose $A$ takes on the values $a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n } \in k$ . Put $R = \mathbf { Z } _ { p } [ x _ { 1 } , \dots , x _ { n } ]$ , and let $R \to k$ be the ring homomorphism satisfying $x _ { i } \mapsto a _ { i }$ . Then $A$ lifts to a matrix $\tilde { A }$ with coefficients in $R$ . For $n \geq 0$ , we have the higher trace $T _ { n } ( { \tilde { A } } ) \in R$ , defined with respect to $\tilde { \mu }$ .

Let $\lambda$ be a partition of $p$ , and consider the quantity $T _ { \lambda } ( { \tilde { A } } ) \in R \otimes { \bf Q }$ defined in Proposition 7.7. One easily sees that the rational numbers appearing in this expression have denominators dividing $p !$ , and so $p ! \cdot T _ { \lambda } ( { \tilde { A } } )$ belongs to $R$ . In fact, if $\lambda$ is not $( 1 ^ { p } )$ or $( p )$ then there are no $p$ ’s in the denominators, and so $p ! \cdot T _ { \lambda } ( { \tilde { A } } ) \in p R$ . Of course, $p ! \cdot T _ { p } ( { \tilde { A } } )$ also belongs to $p R$ . Thus Proposition 7.7 shows

$$
p! \cdot T _ {(1 ^ {p})} (\tilde {A}) + p! \cdot T _ {(p)} (\tilde {A}) \in p R.
$$
Now, we have

$$
p! \cdot T _ {(1 ^ {p})} (\tilde {A}) = \mathrm {t r} (\tilde {A}) ^ {p}, \qquad p! \cdot T _ {(p)} (\tilde {A}) = (- 1) ^ {p + 1} (p - 1)! \cdot \mathrm {t r} (\tilde {A} ^ {p}).
$$
Applying the homomorphism $R \to k$ yields the stated result.
Corollary 7.9. If $k$ is as above and $A \in \operatorname { M a t } _ { X }$ is nilpotent then $\operatorname { t r } ( A ) = 0$ .
Proof. Let $n$ be such that $A ^ { p ^ { \prime \imath } } = 0$ . By Proposition 7.8, we have

$$
\operatorname {t r} (A) ^ {p ^ {n}} = \operatorname {t r} \big (A ^ {p ^ {n}} \big) = 0.
$$
Since $k$ is a field, it follows that $\operatorname { t r } ( A ) = 0$

We thus see that nilpotent matrices have vanishing trace in positive characteristic. We can extend this result to characteristic 0, provided that certain rings have enough maps to fields of positive characteristic. The precise condition we require is the following:

Definition 7.10. A commutative ring $R$ satisfies property ( $P$ ) if for every finitely generated reduced $R$ -algebra $R ^ { \prime }$ we have $\bigcap \ker ( \varphi ) = 0$ , where the intersection is over all homomorphisms $\varphi$ from $R ^ { \prime }$ to fields of positive characteristic. We say that a measure $\mu$ for $G$ satisfies (P) if $\mu ( \Theta ( G ) )$ is contained in a subring of $k$ that satisfies (P). 

We make a few notes concerning this condition. First, if $\mu$ satisfies (P) then any measure obtained from $\mu$ by extension of scalars satisfies (P). In particular, if $\Theta ( G )$ satisfies (P) then any measure satisfies (P). Second, any measure $\mu$ valued in a reduced ring of positive characteristic satisfies (P). And third, if $\mu$ satisfies (P) then so does $\mu | _ { U }$ for any open subgroup $U$ , as $\mu ( \Theta ( U ) )$ is a subring of $\mu ( \Theta ( G ) )$ .
The following is the most general result we are able to prove on traces of nilpotents:
Theorem 7.11. Suppose $k$ is reduced, $\mu$ satisfies (P), and A ∈ MatX is nilpotent. Then $\operatorname { t r } ( A ) = 0$ .
NATE HARMAN AND ANDREW SNOWDEN

Proof. Let $k _ { 0 }$ be a subring of $k$ that contains $\mu ( \Theta ( G ) )$ and satisfies (P), which exists by assumption. The matrix $A$ has only finitely many distinct entries. Let $k _ { 1 } \subset k$ be the $k _ { 0 }$ - subalgebra generated by these entries. We can then regard $A$ as living in $\operatorname { M a t } _ { X } ( k _ { 1 } )$ . For any homomorphism $\varphi \colon k _ { 1 } \to k ^ { \prime }$ with $k ^ { \prime }$ a field of positive characteristic, we have $\varphi ( \operatorname { t r } ( A ) ) = 0$ by Corollary 7.9. Thus $\operatorname { t r } ( A ) = 0$ by definition of (P). 
Remark 7.12. The second author has given an example of a regular measure that does not satisfy (P) for which there exist nilpotent matrices of non-zero trace [Sn3, §1.2(c)]. 

Remark 7.13. One can prove a version of the theorem for the higher traces $T _ { n }$ too. More generally, one can define an analog of the characteristic polynomial of a matrix (using a version of determinant), and prove that it has a particular form. See [HS1, §7] for details. 
7.5. Trace of idempotents. We now examine the higher traces of idempotent matrices:

Proposition 7.14. Suppose $k$ is $\mathbf { Z }$ -flat, let $E \in { \mathrm { M a t } } _ { X }$ be idempotent, and put $a = \operatorname { t r } ( E )$ . Then $\begin{array} { r } { T _ { n } ( E ) = { \binom { a } { n } } } \end{array}$ holds for all $n \geq 0$ . In particular, $\binom { a } { n }$ belongs to $k$ for all $n \geq 0$ .

Proof. Since $k$ is $\mathbf { Z }$ -flat, we can check the identity in $\mathbf { Q } \otimes k$ . Since $E$ is idempotent, we have $\operatorname { t r } ( E ^ { n } ) = a$ for any $n \geq 1$ . The result thus follows from Proposition 7.7, and the polynomial identity

$$
\binom {x} {n} = \sum_ {\lambda \vdash n} \prod_ {j \geq 1} \left[ \frac {1}{m _ {j} !} \left(\frac {(- 1) ^ {j + 1} x}{j}\right) ^ {m _ {j}} \right].
$$

To prove this identity, it suffices to check that the two sides agree when $x = d$ is a positive integer. This in fact follows from Proposition 7.7 by taking $A$ to be the $d \times d$ identity matrix. 

Proposition 7.15. Suppose $k$ is a field of positive characteristic $p$ , and let $E \in { \mathrm { M a t } } _ { X }$ be idempotent. Then there exists a unique $a \in \mathbf { Z } _ { p }$ such that $\begin{array} { r } { T _ { n } ( E ) = { \binom { a } { n } } } \end{array}$ for all $n \geq 0$ .

Proof. We can verify this over an extension field of $k$ , so we assume $k$ is algebraically closed. It follows that the ring $W ( k )$ of Witt vectors is a complete DVR with uniformizer $p$ . Let $U$ be a group of definition for $X$ such that $E$ is $U$ -invariant. We have a surjective algebra homomorphism

$$
\operatorname {M a t} _ {X} ^ {U} (W (k)) \to \operatorname {M a t} _ {X} ^ {U} (k).
$$

(Note: to work with $\operatorname { M a t } _ { X } ( W ( k ) )$ we use the canonical lift of $\mu$ to $W ( k )$ , provided by Corollary 5.2.) Since $\mathrm { M a t } _ { X } ^ { U } ( W ( k ) )$ is a free $W ( k )$ -module of finite rank, it is $p$ -adically complete. Thus we can lift $E$ to an idempotent matrix $\tilde { E }$ in $\mathrm { M a t } _ { X } ^ { U } ( W ( k ) )$ (see [Lam, Theorem 21.28] for lifting modulo $p ^ { n }$ , then take a limit).

Let $a = \operatorname { t r } ( \tilde { E } )$ . By Proposition 7.14, we have ${ \binom { a } { n } } \in W ( k )$ for all $n$ . This implies $a \in \mathbf { Z } _ { p }$ . For instance, letting $\overline { a }$ be the image of $a$ in $k = W ( k ) / ( p )$ , the identity $p { \binom { a } { p } } = a ( a { - } 1 ) \cdot \cdot \cdot ( a { - } p { + } 1 )$ shows that $0 = { \overline { { a } } } ( { \overline { { a } } } - 1 ) \cdot \cdot \cdot ( { \overline { { a } } } - p + 1 )$ , and so $\overline { { a } } \in \mathbf { F } _ { p }$ . By Proposition 7.14, we also have $\begin{array} { r } { T _ { n } ( \tilde { E } ) = \binom { a } { n } } \end{array}$ . Reducing modulo $p$ shows that $\begin{array} { r } { T _ { n } ( E ) = { \binom { a } { n } } } \end{array}$ . 

Definition 7.16. Let $E \in \operatorname { M a t } _ { X }$ be idempotent with $k$ a field of characteristic $p$ . We define the $p$ -adic trace of $E$ to be the value $a \in \mathbf { Z } _ { p }$ given by Proposition 7.15. 

7.6. Invariant algebras. We define the trace pairing on the algebra Mat $X$ by

$$
\langle A, B \rangle = \operatorname {t r} (A B).
$$
A simple computation (see the proof of Proposition 7.6) yields the following explicit expression for the pairing:

$$
\langle A, B \rangle = \int_ {X \times X} A (x, y) B (y, x) d (x, y).
$$

The trace pairing is a symmetric bilinear form on Mat $X$ . Assuming $X$ is a $G$ -set, it induces a symmetric bilinear form on the invariant subalgebra $\mathrm { M a t } _ { X } ^ { G }$ . We now examine this.

where r is the number of transpose-conjugate pairs among the $Z _ { i }$ (see proof ). In particular, the trace pairing is perfect if and only if $\mu ( Z _ { i } )$ is a unit for all $i$ .

Proof. Let $B _ { i } \in \mathrm { M a t } _ { X } ^ { G }$ be the matrix given by $B _ { i } ( x , y ) = 1 _ { Z _ { i } } ( x , y )$ . Since the $1 _ { Z _ { i } }$ clearly form a basis for the $G$ -invariant functions on $X \times X$ , we see that the $B _ { i }$ form a basis for $\mathrm { M a t } _ { X } ^ { G }$ . Let $Z _ { i } ^ { t }$ be the transpose of $Z _ { i }$ , i.e., the set of pairs $( y , x )$ with $( x , y ) \in Z _ { i }$ . Clearly, $Z _ { i } ^ { t }$ is a $G$ -orbit on $X \times X$ , and therefore equal to $Z _ { j }$ for some $j$ . Let $\tau$ be the involution of $\{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ defined by $Z _ { i } ^ { t } = Z _ { \tau ( i ) }$ . We have

$$
\langle B _ {i}, B _ {j} \rangle = \int_ {X \times X} 1 _ {Z _ {i}} (x, y) 1 _ {Z _ {j}} (y, x) d (x, y) = \mathrm {v o l} (Z _ {i} \cap Z _ {\tau (j)}) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \mu (Z _ {i}) & \mathrm {i f} i = \tau (j) \\ 0 & \mathrm {o t h e r w i s e .} \end{array} \right.
$$

We thus see that the matrix for the trace pairing is block diagonal: each fixed point $i$ of $\tau$ contributes a $1 \times 1$ block with entry $\mu ( Z _ { i } )$ , while each pair $i \neq \tau ( i )$ contributes the $2 \times 2$ block

$$
\left( \begin{array}{c c} 0 & \mu (Z _ {i}) \\ \mu (Z _ {i}) & 0 \end{array} \right).
$$
(Note that $Z _ { i }$ and $Z _ { i } ^ { t }$ have the same measure.) The determinant of this matrix is the sign of $\tau$ times the product of the $\mu ( Z _ { i } )$ ’s, which yields the claim. 

(b) For every $G$ -orbit $Z$ on $X \times X$ we have $\mu ( Z ) \neq 0$

Proof. Let $J$ be the Jacobson radical of $\mathrm { M a t } _ { X } ^ { G }$ . Every element of $J$ is nilpotent, and $\mathrm { M a t } _ { X } ^ { G }$ is semi-simple if and only if $J = 0$ . 9. Classification of linearizations

9.1. Overview. Let $G$ be a pro-oligomorphic group. The category $\mathcal { S } ( G )$ of finitary smooth $G$ -sets can be thought of as “non-linear tensor category,” and our category ${ \underline { { \operatorname { P e r m } } } } ( G ; \mu )$ can be seen as a linear version of it. The purpose of §9 is to make this idea precise.

We introduce a rigorous notion of a “linearization” of $\mathcal { S } ( G )$ (Definition 9.8). Roughly speaking, a linearization is a tensor category $\mathbb { T }$ with the same objects as $\mathcal { S } ( G )$ , and where disjoint union and cartesian product in $\mathcal { S } ( G )$ are transformed into direct sum and tensor product in $\mathbb { T }$ . The precise definition is a little more technical, but it is important to underscore that the definition is rather weak (in the sense that it demands little) and, in particular, does not make any reference to the notion of measure or the ring $\Theta ( G )$ .

Our main theorem (Theorem 9.9) asserts that every linearization of $\mathcal { S } ( G )$ is of the form ${ \underline { { \operatorname { P e r m } } } } ( G ; \mu )$ for some measure $\mu$ . The theorem can be reformulated as the following modulitheoretic description of $\Theta ( G )$ (see Corollary 9.10):
Spec $\Theta ( G )$ is the space of linearizations of $\mathcal { S } ( G )$ .
NATE HARMAN AND ANDREW SNOWDEN

We therefore see that the concept of measure and the ring $\Theta ( G )$ are, in a sense, inevitable. For this reason, we view Theorem 9.9 as philosophically important. It is also practically important: it is central to our classification of discrete pre-Tannakian categories in [HS4].
The proofs of the results in §9 are rather lengthy. We therefore state the main definitions and results in §9.2–9.4, and defer the proofs to the end of the section.

9.2. Balanced functors. Our first goal is to describe the $k$ -linear functors out of ${ \underline { { \operatorname { P e r m } } } } ( G ; \mu )$ in terms of the category $\mathcal { S } ( G )$ . We have two natural functors from $\mathcal { S } ( G )$ to ${ \underline { { \operatorname { P e r m } } } } ( G ; \mu )$ : on objects, each takes $X$ to $\operatorname { V e c } _ { X }$ , but on morphisms one takes $f$ to $A _ { f }$ and the other (which is contravariant) takes $f$ to $B _ { f }$ (see §7.7). Thus if we have a $k$ -linear functor $\underline { { \mathrm { P e r m } } } ( G ; \mu ) \to \mathcal { T }$ for some $k$ -linear category $\mathbb { T }$ , we obtain, by composition, two functors from $\mathcal { S } ( G )$ to $\mathbb { T }$ . This is the motivation for Definition 9.1 below.

Before giving the definition, we introduce some notation. For a category $\mathcal { C }$ , we let ${ \mathfrak { C } } ^ { \circ \circ }$ be the maximal groupoid in $\mathcal { C }$ , i.e., the category with the same objects but with morphisms being isomorphisms in $\zeta$ . We note that there is a canonical isomorphism of categories ${ \mathcal C } ^ { \circ } = ( { \mathcal C } ^ { \circ } ) ^ { \mathrm { o p } }$

Definition 9.1. A balanced functor $\mathcal { S } ( G )  \mathcal { T }$ is a pair $( \Phi , \Phi ^ { \prime } )$ of functors $\Phi \colon { \mathcal { S } } ( G ) \to \mathcal { T }$ and $\Phi ^ { \prime } \colon \mathcal { S } ( G ) ^ { \mathrm { o p } } \to \mathcal { T }$ that have equal restriction to $\mathcal { S } ( G ) ^ { \circ } = ( \mathcal { S } ( G ) ^ { \circ } ) ^ { \mathrm { o p } }$ . 
Explicitly, to give a balanced functor we must give for each finitary $G$ -set $X$ an object $\Phi ( X )$ of $\mathbb { T }$ , and for each $G$ -morphism $f \colon X \to Y$ two morphisms

$$
\alpha_ {f} \colon \Phi (X) \to \Phi (Y), \quad \beta_ {f} \colon \Phi (Y) \to \Phi (X).
$$

Here we write $\alpha _ { f }$ in place of $\Phi ( f )$ and $\beta _ { f }$ in place of $\Phi ^ { \prime } ( f )$ ; we will prefer this notation in much of what follows. Formation of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ must be compatible with composition, and we must have $\alpha _ { f } = \beta _ { f } ^ { - 1 }$ whenever $f$ is an isomorphism. The notion of isomorphism of balanced functor is evident.

$$

$$

given on objects by $\Phi _ { \mu } ( X ) = \operatorname { V e c } _ { X }$ and on morphisms by $\alpha _ { f } = A _ { f }$ and $\beta _ { f } = B _ { f }$ , where $A$ and $B$ are as in §7.7. This is the motivating example. 

• A symmetric monoidal balanced functor $\Phi \colon { \mathcal { S } } ( G ) \to { \mathcal { T } }$ is plenary if for every transitive $G$ -set $X$ the $k$ -module ${ \mathrm { H o m } } _ { \mathbb { T } } ( \Phi ( X ) , \mathbb { 1 } )$ is free of rank one with basis $\alpha _ { X }$ .

Definition 9.8. Definition 9.11. A Frobenius algebra in $\mathbb { T }$ is an object $X$ equipped with maps

as maps $X \otimes X \to X \otimes X$ .

Part III. General representations
10. The completed group algebra and its modules

10.1. Overview. In Part III, we define and study an abelian tensor category $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } _ { k } ( G ; \mu )$ associated to a pro-oligomorphic group $G$ and a measure $\mu$ . The main theorem (Theorem 13.2) asserts that this construction results in a rigid tensor category in certain circumstances. The purpose of §10 is simply to construct the abelian category $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ .

We first define a $k$ -algebra $A$ called the completed group algebra of $G$ . We would like to define this as a function space on $G$ under convolution. This is not actually possible, since we do not have a theory of integration for functions on $G$ in general. However, if we imagined that we had such a theory, a function on $G$ would push-forward to one on $G / U$ for each open subgroup $U$ , and we would thereby obtain a compatible sequence of elements of ${ \mathcal { C } } ( G / U )$ as

We do not prove any substantial results about $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ in §10. In fact, we do not know any interesting results about $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ that hold in general: to say anything, we must impose some conditions on the measure $\mu$ . Such results are established in subsequent sections.
We fix a pro-oligomorphic group $G$ and a $k$ -valued measure $\mu$ for the duration §10. Throughout §§10–13 we work in the absolute case; see §13.4 for comments about the relative case.

Proposition 10.7. The category $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ is a Grothendieck abelian category.

Proof. It is clear that if $M$ is a smooth $A$ -module then any sub or quotient of $M$ (as an $A$ -module) is again smooth. Thus $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ is an abelian subcategory of Mod $A$ . Moreover, a direct limit of smooth $A$ -modules is again smooth. It follows that $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ is co-complete, and that direct limits in $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ can be computed in Mod $A$ . In particular, filtered colimits in $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ are exact, and so Grothendieck’s axiom (AB5) holds. Finally, $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ has a generator, namely, the direct sum of all smooth modules of the form $A / I$ with $I$ a left ideal. 

$$

$$
where the directed union is over all open subgroups $U$ of $G$ .

Proof. Suppose $x \in M$ is strictly $U$ -invariant. For $g \in U$ , consider $1 - g \in k | G |$ as an element of $A$ . Its push-forward to ${ \mathcal { C } } ( G / U )$ vanishes. Since $x$ is strictly $U$ -invariant, we therefore have $( 1 - g ) x = 0$ , and so $g x = x$ . This shows that $x$ is $U$ -invariant. 

Remark 10.10. Define a $k \mathopen { } \mathclose \bgroup \left. G \aftergroup \egroup \right\rfloor$ -module to be smooth if every element has open stabilizer. The above proposition shows that any smooth $A$ -module restricts to a smooth $k \mathopen { } \mathclose \bgroup \left. G \aftergroup \egroup \right.$ -module. We warn the reader that an $A$ -module that is smooth as a $k \mathopen { } \mathclose \bgroup \left. G \aftergroup \egroup \right.$ -module may not be smooth as an $A$ -module. The category of smooth $k \mathopen { } \mathclose \bgroup \left. G \aftergroup \egroup \right.$ -modules is currently being examined by Ilia Nekrasov [Nek1]; see also [DLLX]. 

11. Normal measures

11.1. Overview. In the previous section, we defined the representation category $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ . In this section, we introduce the notion of a normal measure (which is weaker than the quasiregular condition introduced in §3.7), and prove a number of fundamental results about $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ assuming normality. Here are some of these results:
NATE HARMAN AND ANDREW SNOWDEN

list_items: • Schwartz space ${ \mathcal { C } } ( X )$ has a mapping property.
• The functor $\Phi$ $\Phi \colon { \underline { { \mathrm { P e r m } } } } ( G ) \to \underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ is fully faithful.
• We establish some fundamental exact sequences involving Schwartz spaces.
• We show that invariants and strict invariants coincide for smooth modules.
• We define some important averaging operators on smooth modules.
• We define a version of integration for module-valued functions.

text: These foundational results are needed to establish the more exciting results about Rep Rep(G) in subsequent sections. In §14.7 we will see counterexamples to many of these results in the non-normal case.

We fix a pro-oligomorphic group $G$ and a $k$ -valued measure $\mu$ throughout §11. We assume for simplicity that $G$ is first-countable, though this is not needed for every result. We note that if $G$ is oligomorphic and $\Omega$ is countable then $G$ is first-countable. From §11.4 onwards, we assume that $\mu$ is normal.
11.2. Normal measures. We now introduce the key concept of §11.

Definition 11.1. We say that the measure $\mu$ is normal if whenever $f \colon X \to Y$ is a surjection of finitary $G$ -sets, the map $f _ { * } \colon { \mathcal { C } } ( X ) \to { \mathcal { C } } ( Y )$ is surjective. 

To verify $f _ { * }$ is surjective, it is enough to realize $1 _ { Y }$ in its image: indeed, if $1 _ { Y } = f _ { * } ( \epsilon )$ , for some $\epsilon \in \mathcal { C } ( X )$ , then for any $\varphi \in \mathcal { C } ( Y )$ we have $\varphi = f _ { * } ( f ^ { * } ( \varphi ) \cdot \epsilon )$ by the projection formula (Proposition 4.11). From this, we see that normality is preserved under extension of scalars. (Given $k  k ^ { \prime }$ and a surjection $f \colon X \to Y$ , choose a lift of $1 _ { Y }$ to a $k$ -valued Schwartz function $\varphi$ on $X$ . Then the extension of scalars of $\varphi$ to $k ^ { \prime }$ is a lift of $1 _ { Y }$ as a $k ^ { \prime }$ -valued function.)

While the condition defining normality appears to be very plausible, there are cases where it does not hold. In particular, it often seems to fail in positive characteristic. See §14.7 for an explicit example in the case of the symmetric group.
We now establish two basic results concerning normality.
Proposition 11.2. For $U \subset G$ an open subgroup, $\mu$ is normal if and only if $\mu | _ { U }$ is.

Proof. Suppose $\mu | _ { U }$ is normal and let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a surjection of finitary $G$ -sets. Then $f$ is also a surjection of finitary $U$ -sets, and so $f _ { * }$ is surjective. Thus $\mu$ is normal.

Now suppose that $\mu$ is normal. Let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a surjection of finitary $U$ -sets and let $\varphi \in \mathcal { C } ( Y )$ be given. Let ${ \tilde { X } } = I _ { U } ^ { G } ( X )$ and $Y = I _ { U } ^ { G } ( Y )$ be the inductions of $X$ and $Y$ to $G$ (see §2.4), and let $\tilde { f } \colon \tilde { X }  \tilde { Y }$ be the induced map. We have a commutative diagram of $G$ -sets

and $X$ and $Y$ are identified with the fibers over $1 \in G / U$ ; in particular, $\tilde { f } ^ { - 1 } ( Y ) = X$ . Now, regard $\varphi$ as a function on $\tilde { Y }$ by extending it to 0 outside of $Y$ . As such, it is still a smooth function. Since $\mu$ is normal, there is some $\psi \in \mathcal { C } ( \tilde { X } )$ such that $\tilde { f } _ { * } ( \psi ) = \varphi$ . Since the only points above $Y$ belong to $X$ , it follows that $f _ { * } ( \psi | _ { X } ) = \varphi$ . Thus $\mu | _ { U }$ is normal. 
Recall the notion of (quasi-)regular measure from Definition 3.18.
OLIGOMORPHIC GROUPS AND TENSOR CATEGORIES
Proposition 11.3. If µ is quasi-regular then it is normal.

Proof. Let $U$ be an open subgroup such that $\mu | _ { U }$ is regular. Let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a surjection of $U$ -sets. We claim that $f _ { * }$ is surjective. We can consider each orbit on $Y$ separately, and thereby reduce to the case where $Y$ is transitive. And we can discard all but one orbit on $X$ , and thus assume $X$ is transitive. Since $\mu | _ { U }$ is regular, we have $f _ { * } ( c ^ { - 1 } 1 _ { X } ) = 1 _ { Y }$ , where $c = \mu ( X ) / \mu ( Y )$ is a unit of $k$ , and so $f _ { * }$ is surjective (see comments following Definition 11.1). We thus see that $\mu | _ { U }$ is normal, and so $\mu$ is normal by Proposition 11.2. 
In §14.8, we give an example in the relative case of a measure that is normal and not quasi-regular. We know of no such example in the absolute case.

11.3. Characterizations of normality. We now give two alternate characterizations of normality (see [HS1, §14.2] for a third). The first one is the main reason normality is so useful in studying $A$ -modules.
Proposition 11.4. The following conditions are equivalent:

list_items: (a) The measure $\mu$ is normal.
(b) For every open subgroup $U$ of $G$ , the natural map $A \to \mathcal { C } ( G / U )$ is surjective.

text: Proof. First suppose (a) holds. Then the transition maps $\pi _ { U , V }$ in the inverse limit defining $A$ are surjective. Since $G$ is first-countable, the inverse limit can be taken over a countable cofinal family of open subgroups. Condition (b) now follows from the following general fact: if $X _ { \bullet }$ is a countably indexed inverse system of sets with surjective transition maps then the map $\varprojlim { X _ { \bullet } }  X _ { i }$ is surjective for each $i$ .

Now suppose (b) holds. Let $V \subset U$ be open subgroups of $G$ . Then the surjective map $A \to \mathcal { C } ( G / U )$ factors through ${ \mathcal { C } } ( G / V )$ , and so wee see that $\pi _ { V , U } \colon \mathcal { C } ( G / V ) \to \mathcal { C } ( G / U )$ is surjective. It follows that if $f \colon Y \to X$ is any map of transitive $G$ -sets then $f _ { * }$ is surjective. Normality follows easily from this. 

Remark 11.5. Suppose $\mu$ is regular. Let $V \subset U$ be open subgroups, and let $f \colon G / V \to G / U$ be the natural map. Then $\mu ( U / V ) ^ { - 1 } f ^ { * }$ provides a canonical section to $f _ { * }$ (by the projection formula Proposition 4.11). From this, one can show Proposition 11.4(b) holds even if $G$ is not first-countable. This argument can be adapted to the quasi-regular case as well. 
Our next result is a matrix-theoretic interpretation of normality.
Proposition 11.6. The following conditions are equivalent:

list_items: (a) The measure $\mu$ is normal.

(b) Given a surjection $f \colon Y \to X$ of finitary $\hat { G }$ -sets, the matrix $A _ { f } \in \operatorname { M a t } _ { X , Y }$ has a right inverse, i.e., there is a matrix $C \in \mathrm { M a t } _ { Y , X }$ such that $A _ { f } \cdot C = I _ { X }$ .

text: Proof. First suppose that (b) holds. Let $f \colon Y \to X$ of finitary $\hat { G }$ -sets. We claim that $f _ { * } \colon { \mathcal { C } } ( Y ) \to { \mathcal { C } } ( X )$ is surjective. To see this, let $w \in \operatorname { V e c } _ { X }$ be given. Putting $v = C w$ , where $C$ is the right-inverse to $A _ { f }$ , we have $A _ { f } v = w$ . But $A _ { f } v = f _ { * } ( v )$ by Proposition 7.20, and so the claim follows. Thus $\mu$ is normal.

Now suppose (a) holds. Let $f \colon Y \to X$ be a surjection of finitary $\hat { G }$ -sets. Let $U$ be a group of definition for $X$ and $Y$ such that $f$ is $U$ -equivariant. Since $\mu | _ { U }$ is normal (Proposition 11.2), there is a function $\epsilon \in \mathcal { C } ( Y )$ such that $f _ { * } ( \epsilon ) = 1 _ { X }$ . Let $C$ be the matrix given by $C ( y , x ) =$

$\epsilon ( y ) B _ { f } ( y , x )$ . For $v \in { \mathrm { V e c } } _ { X }$ , we have

$$
(C v) (y) = \int_ {X} C (y, x) v (x) d x = \epsilon (y) \left(B _ {f} v\right) (y).
$$
We thus have $C v = \epsilon \cdot f ^ { * } ( v )$ by Proposition 7.20. Therefore,

$$
A _ {f} C v = f _ {*} (\epsilon \cdot f ^ {*} (v)) = v \cdot f _ {*} (\epsilon) = v,
$$

where in the first step we used Proposition 7.20, in the second the projection formula (Proposition 4.11), and in the third the defining property of $\epsilon$ . We thus have $A _ { f } C = I _ { X }$ by Proposition 7.5, and so (b) holds. 
Remark 11.7. We make three remarks concerning the above proposition:

list_items: (a) If $f$ is a map of $G$ -sets then the matrix $A _ { f }$ is $G$ -invariant. However, we cannot necessarily take $C$ to be $G$ -invariant.

(b) Taking transpose, condition (b) is equivalent to the matrix $B _ { f }$ having a left inverse. Note that if $f \colon X \to Y$ is a surjection of $G$ -sets then $f ^ { * }$ is always injective. However, we need normality to conclude $B _ { f }$ has a left inverse matrix (in general).

(c) Suppose $\mu$ is regular, let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a surjection of transitive $G$ -sets, and let $c$ b e the common measure of fibers of $f$ . Similar to Remark 11.5, we see that $C = c ^ { - 1 } B _ { f }$ is a right inverse to $A _ { f }$ . We thus have an explicit $G$ -invariant right inverse to $A _ { f }$ . 

text: 11.4. Schwartz spaces. We assume for the remainder of §11 that the measure $\mu$ is normal. We now establish some basic properties of Schwartz spaces.

Proposition 11.8. Let $X$ be a $G$ -set and let $\{ x _ { i } \} _ { i \in I }$ be representatives for the $G$ -orbits on $X$ . Then the point masses $\delta _ { X , x _ { i } }$ generate ${ \mathcal { C } } ( X )$ as an $A$ -module.

Proof. It suffices to treat the case where $X = G / U$ for some open subgroup $U$ , and show that the point-mass $\delta _ { 1 }$ at $1 \in G / U$ generates ${ \mathcal { C } } ( G / U )$ . Since $\delta _ { 1 }$ is left $U$ -invariant, for $a \in A$ we have

We therefore find $a \delta _ { 1 } = a _ { U }$ . Thus given any function $\varphi \in \mathcal { C } ( X )$ , we have $\varphi = a \delta _ { 1 }$ where $a$ is any element of $A$ with $\boldsymbol { a } _ { U } = \boldsymbol { \varphi }$ ; such an $a$ exists by Proposition 11.4. We thus see that $\dot { \delta _ { 1 } }$ generates, as required. 
Corollary 11.9. If $X$ is a finitary $G$ -set then ${ \mathcal { C } } ( X )$ is a finitely generated A-module.
Proposition 11.10. Let $M$ be an arbitrary $A$ -module and let $U$ be an open subgroup of $G$ We then have an isomorphism

$$
\Phi \colon \operatorname {H o m} _ {A} (\mathcal {C} (G / U), M) \to M ^ {s U}, \qquad \Phi (f) = f (\delta_ {1}).
$$

Proof. The function $\delta _ { 1 }$ is a strictly $U$ -invariant element of ${ \mathcal { C } } ( G / U )$ . It follows that if $f \colon { \mathcal { C } } ( G / U ) \to M$ is a map of $A$ -modules then $f ( \delta _ { 1 } )$ is also strictly $U$ -invariant. Thus $\Phi$ is a well-defined function. The element $\delta _ { 1 }$ generates ${ \mathcal { C } } ( G / U )$ by Proposition 11.8, and so $\Phi$ is injective. It remains to prove that $\Phi$ is surjective.

Let $x \in M ^ { s U }$ be given. We define a function $f \colon { \mathcal { C } } ( G / U ) \to M$ by $f ( \overline { { a } } ) = a x$ where $a$ is any lift of $\overline { a }$ to $A$ . We note that a lift exists by Proposition 11.4, and the element $u x$ is independent of the choice of $a$ since $x$ is strictly $U$ -invariant. If ${ \overline { { a } } } \in { \mathcal { C } } ( G / U )$ and $b \in A$ then $b a$ is a lift of $b \overline { { a } }$ , since the map $A \to \mathcal { C } ( G / U )$ is $A$ -linear (see the discussion following

Proposition 10.11). It follows that $f ( b { \overline { { a } } } ) = b a x = b f ( { \overline { { a } } } )$ , and so $f$ is a map of $A$ -modules. As $\Phi ( f ) = x$ , we see that $\Phi$ is surjective, which completes the proof. 

Proposition 11.11. Let M be a smooth A-module. Then there is a $G$ -set $X$ and a surjection $\mathcal { C } ( X )  M$ of A-modules. One can take $X$ finitary if and only if $M$ is finitely generated.

Proof. Let $\{ x _ { i } \} _ { i \in I }$ be a generating set for $M$ as an $A$ -module. Let $U _ { i }$ be an open subgroup such that $x _ { i }$ is strictly $U _ { i }$ -invariant. By Proposition 11.10, we have a map $\mathcal { C } ( G / U _ { i } ) \to M$ of $A$ -modules that takes $\delta _ { 1 }$ to $x _ { i }$ . We thus obtain a surjection $\mathcal { C } ( X )  M$ with $\textstyle X = \coprod _ { i \in I } G / U _ { i }$ . If $M$ is finitely generated, we can take $I$ to be finite, and then $X$ is finitary. Conversely, if we have a surjection $\mathcal { C } ( X )  M$ with $X$ finitary then $M$ is finitely generated since ${ \mathcal { C } } ( X )$ is (Corollary 11.9). 
11.5. Towards abelian envelopes. Recall (Proposition 10.13) we have a faithful functor

$$
\Phi \colon \underline {{\mathrm {P e r m}}} (G) \to \underline {{\mathrm {R e p}}} (G).
$$
We now establish some necessary properties for $\Phi$ to be an abelian envelope. See Theorem 13.13 for a more definitive result.
Proposition 11.12. The functor $\Phi$ is full.
Proof. Let $X$ and $Y$ be finitary $G$ -sets. We must show that the map
is surjective. It suffices to treat the case $X = G / U$ , so we assume this in what follows. By definition of Perm(G), we have

$$
\operatorname {H o m} (\operatorname {V e c} _ {X}, \operatorname {V e c} _ {Y}) = \operatorname {M a t} _ {Y, X} ^ {G} = \operatorname {F u n} (G \backslash (X \times Y), k).
$$
We also have

$$
\mathrm {H o m} _ {A} (\mathcal {C} (X), \mathcal {C} (Y)) = \mathcal {C} (Y) ^ {s U} = \mathcal {C} (Y) ^ {U} = \mathrm {F u n} (G \backslash (X \times Y), k).
$$

The first identification above is Proposition 11.10, the second comes from the definition of the $A$ -module structure on ${ \mathcal { C } } ( Y )$ , and the third comes from the isomorphism $G \backslash ( X \times Y ) = U \backslash Y$ . We thus see that the domain and target in (11.13) are canonically identified. One can now argue that, under these identifications, $\Phi$ is the identity. Alternatively, one can argue as follows. First suppose $k$ is a field. Then (11.13) is an injection of vector spaces of the same finite dimension, and so it is necessarily surjective. The general case follows from the field case, since the source and target in (11.13) are free modules of the same finite rank (look at the determinant). 

11.6. Some exact sequences. We now establish some fundamental exact sequences involving Schwartz spaces. These results crucially rely upon the normality of the measure. We use these sequences in §11.7 to compare invariants and strict invariants.
Proposition 11.14. Consider a cartesian square
NATE HARMAN AND ANDREW SNOWDEN
of finitary $G$ -sets, with $f$ and $g$ surjective. Then the sequence

$$
\mathcal {C} \left(X ^ {\prime}\right) \xrightarrow {g _ {*} ^ {\prime} + f _ {*} ^ {\prime}} \mathcal {C} (X) \oplus \mathcal {C} \left(Y ^ {\prime}\right) \xrightarrow {f _ {*} - g _ {*}} \mathcal {C} (Y) \longrightarrow 0
$$
is exact.

Proof. Since $f$ is surjective, so is $f _ { * }$ (by normality of $\mu$ ), and so $f _ { * } - g _ { * }$ is also surjective. By transitivity of push-forward (Proposition 4.8), we have $f _ { * } g _ { * } ^ { \prime } = g _ { * } f _ { * } ^ { \prime }$ , and so the first two maps in the sequence compose to zero.

Now suppose we have $\varphi \in \mathcal { C } ( X )$ and $\psi \in \mathcal { C } ( Y ^ { \prime } )$ satisfying $f _ { * } ( \varphi ) = g _ { * } ( \psi )$ , so that $( \varphi , \psi )$ is a typical element of $\ker ( f _ { * } - g _ { * } )$ . We must show that $( \varphi , \psi )$ belongs to the image of $g _ { * } ^ { \prime } + f _ { * } ^ { \prime }$ . Since $g ^ { \prime }$ is surjective, so is $g _ { * } ^ { \prime }$ (by normality), and so we can find $\tilde { \varphi } \in \mathcal { C } ( X ^ { \prime } )$ with $g _ { * } ^ { \prime } ( \tilde { \varphi } ) = \varphi$ . Without loss of generality, we may as well replace $( \varphi , \psi )$ with $( \varphi , \psi ) - ( g _ { * } ^ { \prime } ( \tilde { \varphi } ) , f _ { * } ^ { \prime } ( \tilde { \varphi } ) )$ , and thereby assume $\varphi = 0$ in what follows.

Appealing to normality again, let $\epsilon \in \mathcal { C } ( X )$ satisfy $f _ { * } ( \epsilon ) = 1 _ { Y }$ . Let $\eta = ( f ^ { \prime } ) ^ { * } ( \psi ) \cdot ( g ^ { \prime } ) ^ { * } ( \epsilon )$ . We have

$$
f _ {*} ^ {\prime} (\eta) = \psi \cdot f _ {*} ^ {\prime} ((g ^ {\prime}) ^ {*} (\epsilon)) = \psi \cdot g ^ {*} (f _ {*} (\epsilon)) = \psi \cdot 1 _ {Y ^ {\prime}} = \psi
$$
where in the first step we used the projection formula (Proposition 4.11) and in the second step base change (Proposition 4.12). We also have

$$
g _ {*} ^ {\prime} (\eta) = \epsilon \cdot g _ {*} ^ {\prime} ((f ^ {\prime}) ^ {*} (\psi)) = \epsilon \cdot f ^ {*} (g _ {*} (\psi)) = 0,
$$

again by the projection formula and base change. Note that $g _ { * } ( \psi ) = 0$ since $( 0 , \psi )$ belongs to the kernel of $f _ { * } - g _ { * }$ . Thus $( 0 , \psi ) = ( g _ { * } ^ { \prime } ( \eta ) , f _ { * } ^ { \prime } ( \eta ) )$ , and so $( 0 , \psi )$ is in the image of $f _ { * } ^ { \prime } + g _ { * } ^ { \prime }$ . This completes the proof. 
Corollary 11.15. Let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a surjection of finitary $G$ -sets, and let $p , q \colon X \times _ { Y } X \to$ $X$ be the two projections. Then the sequence

$$
\mathcal {C} (X \times_ {Y} X) \xrightarrow {p _ {*} - q _ {*}} \mathcal {C} (X) \xrightarrow {f _ {*}} \mathcal {C} (Y) \longrightarrow 0
$$
is exact. In particular, $\ker ( f _ { * } )$ is generated, as an A-module, by the elements $\delta _ { w } - \delta _ { x }$ where $w , x \in X$ satisfy $f ( w ) = f ( x )$ .

Proof. As in the proposition, $f _ { * }$ is surjective and the two maps compose to zero. Suppose now that $\varphi \in \mathcal { C } ( X )$ satisfies $f _ { * } ( \varphi ) = 0$ . Then $( \varphi , 0 )$ belongs to the kernel of the map

$$
\left(f _ {*}, - f _ {*}\right): \mathcal {C} (X) \oplus \mathcal {C} (X) \to \mathcal {C} (Y).
$$

Thus, by the proposition, there is $\psi \in \mathcal { C } ( X \times _ { Y } X )$ such that $( \varphi , 0 ) = ( p _ { * } ( \psi ) , q _ { * } ( \psi ) )$ , and so $\varphi = p _ { * } ( \psi ) - q _ { * } ( \psi )$ belongs to the image of $p _ { * } - q _ { * }$ . This shows that the sequence is exact. The statement about generators follows since the elements $\delta _ { ( w , x ) }$ generate $\mathcal { C } ( X \times _ { Y } X )$ by Proposition 11.8. 

11.7. Invariants and strict invariants. We now show that invariants and strict invariants coincide for a smooth module. This allows us to improve the mapping property for Schwartz spaces, and is also a crucial ingredient for the version of integration defined in §11.9 (see Remark 11.27).
Proposition 11.16. Let M be a smooth A-module and let $U$ be an open subgroup of $G$ . Then
That is, an element of M is strictly U-invariant if and only if it is U-invariant.
OLIGOMORPHIC GROUPS AND TENSOR CATEGORIES

Proof. Let $x \in M$ be given. We have already seen that if $x$ is strictly $U$ -invariant then it is $U$ -invariant (Proposition 10.9). Suppose now that $x$ is $U$ -invariant. Let $V \subset U$ be an open subgroup such that $x$ is strictly $V$ -invariant, and let $f \colon G / V \to G / U$ be the natural map. By Proposition 11.10, we have a map $h \colon { \mathfrak { C } } ( G / V ) \to M$ of $A$ -modules given by $h ( \overline { { a } } ) = a x$ , where $a$ is any lift of $\overline { a }$ to $A$ . For $g \in G$ and $u \in U$ , we have

$$
h (\delta_ {G / V, g} - \delta_ {G / V, g u}) = g x - g u x = 0

12. Tensor products

12.1. Overview. In this section, we define a tensor structure on the category $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ . There is a formal approach to this: one can declare ${ \mathfrak { C } } ( X ) \otimes { \mathfrak { C } } ( Y ) = { \mathfrak { C } } ( X \times Y )$ by fiat, and then extend $\bigotimes$ to all of $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ by choosing presentations by Schwartz spaces. While it is possible to carry out this plan, it is rather unenlightening since it does not attached any meaning to the tensor product of two modules.

We take a more organic approach: given two smooth $A$ -modules $M$ and $N$ , we define a tensor product to be a smooth $A$ -module $T$ equipped with a universal “strongly bilinear” map $M \times N  T$ . Strongly bilinear means that in each variable the map is $k \mathopen { } \mathclose \bgroup \left. G \aftergroup \egroup \right\rfloor$ -linear and also commutes with integrals. The main result of this section (Theorem 12.9) asserts that the tensor products always exist, and that $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ therefore has the structure of a tensor

category. We give a similar treatment to internal Hom, and show that the usual tensor-Hom adjunction holds.
We fix a first-countable pro-oligomorphic group $G$ and a $k$ -valued normal measure $\mu$ for the duration of §12.
12.2. Strongly bilinear maps. Our notion of tensor product is based on the following notion of bi-linearity for $A$ -modules:
Definition 12.1. Let $M$ , $N$ , and $E$ be smooth $A$ -modules, and consider a function

$$
q \colon M \times N \to E.
$$
We say that $q$ is strongly bilinear if it satisfies the following conditions:

list_items: (a) $q$ is $k$ -bilinear.
(b) $q$ is $G$ -equivariant, that is, $q ( g m , g n ) = g q ( m , n )$ for $g \in G$ , $m \in M$ , and $n \in N$ .
(c) Given finitary $G$ -sets $X$ and $Y$ and smooth functions $\varphi \colon X \to M$ and $\psi \colon Y  N$ , we have

text:
$$
q \left(\int_ {X} \varphi (x) d x, \int_ {Y} \psi (y) d y\right) = \int_ {X \times Y} q (\varphi (x), \psi (y)) d (x, y).
$$
Note that $( x , y ) \mapsto q ( \varphi ( x ) , \psi ( y ) )$ is smooth by (b), and so the integral on the right side is well-defined. 

The most subtle aspect of the above definition is condition (c). We now discuss it in some more detail. Fix a map $q$ as above, and assume that it satisfies (a) and (b). We say that $q$ is strongly linear in the first parameter if for any smooth function $\varphi \colon X \to M$ and any $n \in N$ we have

$$
q \left(\int_ {X} \varphi (x) d x, n\right) = \int_ {X} q (\varphi (x), n) d x
$$
Strongly linear in the second variable is defined similarly. It is easy to see that $q$ satisfies (c) if and only if it is strongly linear in each variable.
