12.3. The definition of tensor product. We now arrive at the notion of tensor product:

Definition 12.3. Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth $A$ -modules. A tensor product of $M$ and $N$ is a smooth $A$ -module $T$ equipped with a strongly bilinear map $q \colon M \times N  T$ that is universal, in the sense that if $q ^ { \prime } \colon M \times N \to T ^ { \prime }$ is any other strongly bilinear map to a smooth $A$ -module then there is a unique map $f \colon T  T ^ { \prime }$ of $A$ -modules such that $q ^ { \prime } = f \circ q$ . 

Suppose that a tensor product of $M$ and $N$ exists. By the universal property, any two tensor products are canonically isomorphic, so we can speak of the tensor product of $M$ and $N$ ; we denote it by $M \otimes N$ . For $x \in M$ and $y \in N$ , we write $x \otimes y$ for the image of $( x , y ) \in M \times N$ under the universal strongly bilinear map $q$ . These elements are the pure tensors in $M \otimes N$ . Given finitary $G$ -sets $X$ and $Y$ and smooth functions $\varphi \colon X \to M$ and $\psi \colon Y  N$ , we have the identity

$$
\left(\int_ {X} \varphi (x) d x\right) \underline {{\otimes}} \left(\int_ {Y} \psi (y) d y\right) = \int_ {X \times Y} \left(\varphi (x) \underline {{\otimes}} \psi (y)\right) d (x, y).
$$
This is simply a restatement of Definition 12.1(c).
We now establish a few simple properties of tensor products.

13. (Quasi-)regular measures

13.1. Overview. So far, assuming $\mu$ is normal, we have constructed an abelian tensor category $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ . In this section, we establish various finer results about $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ assuming $\mu$ is quasi-regular or regular. In particular, we show that the category of finite length objects in $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ forms a rigid tensor category under some hypotheses.

Throughout this section, $G$ denotes a first-countable pro-oligomorphic group and $\mu$ a $k$ - valued measure. The measure $\mu$ will always be regular or quasi-regular (see Definition 3.7), and $k$ will always be a field.
13.2. The main theorem. Before stating our theorem, we introduce some terminology:

We now come to our the main result of §13:

Theorem 13.2. Suppose that $k$ is a field, and $\mu$ is quasi-regular and satisfies condition (P) from Definition 7.10. Then Rep Rep(G) is locally pre-Tannakian. Moreover, if $\mu$ is regular then it is semi-simple.

It is possible to weaken the hypotheses of the theorem in various ways. For example, (P) is only used to ensure nilpotent matrices have trace 0, so one could use this condition instead. We note that in the regular case, the theorem implies that $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ^ { \mathrm { f } } ( G )$ is the Karoubian envelope of Perm(G).
We assume $k$ is a field and $\mu$ is quasi-regular and satisfies (P) for the remainder of §13.2. We break the proof into a number of lemmas.

Lemma 13.3. Let $\mathcal { C }$ be a $k$ -linear Grothendieck abelian category such that every object is the union of its finitely generated subobjects. Let Σ be class of finitely generated objects of C such that
(a) $\Sigma$ is closed under finite direct sums.
NATE HARMAN AND ANDREW SNOWDEN

list_items: (b) Every finitely generated object of $\mathcal { C }$ is a quotient of an object in $\Sigma$ .
(c) End(M) is a finite dimensional semi-simple $k$ -algebra for every $M \in \Sigma$ .

text: Then $\mathcal { C }$ is a semi-simple category, and $\operatorname { E n d } ( M )$ is finite dimensional over $k$ for all finite length objects $M$ .

Proof. Let $E$ be an object of $\Sigma$ . Put $R = \operatorname { E n d } ( E )$ , and consider a subobject of $E$ of the form $a E$ with $a \in R$ . Since $R$ is semi-simple, the right ideal $a R$ is generated by an idempotent $e$ . Thus we have $a = e x$ and $e = a y$ for $x , y \in R$ . It follows that $e E \subset a E \subset e E$ , and so $a { \cal E } = e { \cal E }$ . In particular, we see that $a E$ is a summand of $E$ .

Now suppose $M$ is a finitely generated subobject of $E$ . Choose a surjection $f \colon F \to M$ with $F \in \Sigma$ . Let $a \in \operatorname { E n d } ( E \oplus F )$ be the endomorphism defined by $a ( x ) = f ( x )$ for $x \in F$ and $a ( y ) = 0$ for $y \in E$ . Then $M = a ( E \oplus F )$ . By the previous paragraph, $M$ is a summand of $E \oplus F$ , and thus of $E$ . We have thus shown that every finitely generated subobject of $E$ is a summand.

Suppose now that $0 \subsetneq M _ { 1 } \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq M _ { n } \subsetneq E$ is a chain of finitely generated subobjects. We can then write $E = N _ { 1 } \oplus \cdots \oplus N _ { n + 1 }$ so that $M _ { i } = N _ { 1 } \oplus \cdot \cdot \cdot \oplus N _ { i }$ ; note that $N _ { 1 } , \ldots , N _ { n }$ are non-zero. By considering the projectors onto the $N _ { i }$ ’s, we see that $\dim ( \operatorname { E n d } ( E ) ) \geq n$ . Since $\operatorname { E n d } ( E )$ is finite dimensional, it follows that $E$ has finite length. Thus every subobject is finitely generated, and therefore a summand, and so $E$ is semi-simple. Since every object of $\mathrm { { \small ~  ~ } }$ is a quotient of a sum of objects in $\Sigma$ , it follows that $\mathcal { C }$ is semi-simple.

As for the final statement, suppose that $M$ is a finite length object of $\mathcal { C }$ . Then, by assumption, $M$ is a quotient of some $E \in \Sigma$ . By semi-simplicity, $M$ is actually a summand of $E$ . Thus $\operatorname { E n d } ( M )$ is a summand of $\operatorname { E n d } ( E )$ , and hence finite dimensional. 
Lemma 13.4. If $\mu$ is regular then Rep Rep(G) is semi-simple, and $\operatorname { E n d } ( M )$ is finite dimensional if M has finite length.

Proof. We apply Lemma 13.3 with $\Sigma$ the class of all modules of the form ${ \mathcal { C } } ( X )$ with $X$ a finitary $G$ -set. We must verify the three conditions of the lemma. Condition (a) is clear, while (b) follows from Proposition 11.11. As for (c), we have $\operatorname { E n d } _ { A } ( { \mathcal { C } } ( X ) ) = \operatorname { M a t } _ { X } ^ { G }$ by Proposition 11.12, and this algebra is semi-simple by Proposition 7.19. The result follows. 
Lemma 13.5. Rep Rep(G) is locally of finite length, and End(M) is finite dimensional if $M$ has finite length.

Proof. Let $U$ be an open subgroup such that $\mu | _ { U }$ is regular; note that $\mu | _ { U }$ still satisfies (P) (see the discussion following Definition 7.10). If $M$ is a finitely generated smooth $A ( G )$ -module then it is finitely generated as an $A ( U )$ -module (this follows easily from Proposition 11.11), and thus finite length as an $A ( U )$ -module by Lemma 13.4. Hence it is finite length as an $A ( G )$ -module. Moreover, $\operatorname { E n d } _ { A ( G ) } ( M )$ is a subalgebra of $\operatorname { E n d } _ { A ( U ) } ( M )$ , and is thus finite dimensional by Lemma 13.4. 

It now remains to prove that $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ^ { \mathrm { f } } ( G )$ is pre-Tannakian. Condition (a) of Definition 13.1 holds tautologically for this category. Condition (b) follows from the above lemma, since $\mathrm { H o m } ( M , N )$ injects into $\operatorname { E n d } ( M \oplus N )$ . Also, (c) follows easily from the above results. If $U$ is an open subgroup for which $\mu | _ { U }$ is regular then $1 \in \underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( U )$ is semi-simple and has $\operatorname { E n d } _ { A ( U ) } ( \mathbb { 1 } ) = k$ , and is thus simple; hence $^ { 1 \Vert }$ is simple in $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ as well. The proof of Theorem 13.2 shows that the dual of a finite length object $M$ is given by $\underline { { \mathrm { H o m } } } ( M , \mathbb { 1 } )$ , which is (essentially) the space of smooth vectors in the ordinary dual space $M ^ { * }$ . 13.3. Abelian envelopes. We recall the notion of abelian envelope for tensor categories proposed in [CEAH, Definition 3.1.2]:

Definition 13.12. Let $\mathcal { P }$ be a $k$ -linear tensor category. An abelian envelope of $\mathcal { P }$ is a pair $( \mathcal { R } , \Phi )$ , where $\mathcal { R }$ is a pre-Tannakian category and $\Phi$ is a tensor functor, such that for any pre-Tannakian category $\mathbb { T }$ the functor

$$
\operatorname {F u n} _ {\otimes} ^ {\mathrm {e x}} (\mathcal {R}, \mathfrak {T}) \to \operatorname {F u n} _ {\otimes} ^ {\text {f a i t h}} (\mathcal {P}, \mathfrak {T}), \quad \Psi \mapsto \Psi \circ \Phi
$$

is an equivalence, where Fun $\mathbf { \Sigma } _ { \otimes } ^ { \mathrm { e x } }$ denotes the category of exact tensor functors and $\mathrm { F u n } _ { \otimes } ^ { \mathrm { f a i t h } }$ nfaith the category of faithful tensor functors. 

We note that an abelian envelope is unique up to canonical equivalence when it exists, so we can speak of “the” abelian envelope. With this definition, we can now formulate a precise result for when and how $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G )$ is an abelian envelope of Perm(G).

14. The symmetric group

14.1. Overview. Let $\mathfrak { S }$ be the infinite symmetric group, which we take to be the group of all permutations of the set $\Omega = \{ 1 , 2 , \dots \}$ . In §14, we examine the theory developed in this paper in this case. We show that our work recover Deligne’s interpolation category $\mathrm { R e p } ( \mathfrak { S } _ { t } )$ and some known results about it (e.g., the theorem of Comes–Ostrik [CO2] on abelian envelopes). We also examine what happens in positive characteristic, and observe some pathological behavior.

14.2. Subgroup structure. For $n \in \mathbf N$ , let ${ \mathfrak { S } } _ { n }$ be the usual finite symmetric group, regarded as a subgroup of $\mathfrak { S }$ , and let ${ \mathfrak { S } } ( n )$ be the subgroup of $\mathfrak { S }$ fixing the numbers $1 , \ldots , n$ . Thus $\mathfrak { S } _ { n } \times \mathfrak { S } ( n )$ is a Young subgroup of $\mathfrak { S }$ , and the ${ \mathfrak { S } } ( n )$ ’s form a neighborhood basis of the identity in $\mathfrak { S }$ . The following important proposition gives the structure of open subgroups of $\mathfrak { S }$ . It is likely well-known (see, e.g., [Sci, Proposition A.4] for the analogous statement for finite symmetric groups), but we include a proof for the sake of completeness.
NATE HARMAN AND ANDREW SNOWDEN

Proposition 14.1. Let $U$ be an open subgroup of $\mathfrak { S }$ . Then there exists an integer $n \geq 0$ and a subgroup $H$ of ${ \mathfrak { S } } _ { n }$ such that $U$ is conjugate to $H \times \mathfrak { S } ( n )$ .
Proof. Let $n \geq 0$ be minimal such that ${ \mathfrak { S } } ( n )$ is contained in a conjugate of $U$ . Replacing $U$ with a conjugate, we simply assume that $\mathfrak { S } ( n ) \subset U$ .

We claim that $U$ is contained in ${ \mathfrak { S } } _ { n } \times { \mathfrak { S } } ( n )$ . Suppose not, and let $g$ be an element of $U$ not contained in ${ \mathfrak { S } } _ { n } \times { \mathfrak { S } } ( n )$ . Let $g = \sigma \tau _ { 1 } \cdot \cdot \cdot \tau _ { r }$ be a decomposition of $g$ into disjoint cycles such that $\sigma$ does not belong to ${ \mathfrak { S } } _ { n } \times { \mathfrak { S } } ( n )$ . Write

$$
\sigma = \left(a _ {1} a _ {2} \dots a _ {k}\right)
$$

where $a _ { 1 } > n$ and $a _ { 2 } \leq n$ . Let $a _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } > n$ be an integer not appearing in any cycle in $g$ . Since the transposition $( a _ { 1 } \ a _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } )$ belongs to ${ \mathfrak { S } } ( n )$ , it belongs to $U$ , and so the conjugate $g ^ { \prime }$ of $g$ by this transposition also belong to $U$ . We have $g ^ { \prime } = \sigma ^ { \prime } \tau _ { 1 } \cdot \cdot \cdot \tau _ { r }$ , where $\sigma ^ { \prime }$ is like $\sigma$ but with $a _ { 1 }$ changed to $a _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$ . We thus see that $U$ contains the 3-cycle

$$
g ^ {\prime} g ^ {- 1} = \left(a _ {1} a _ {1} ^ {\prime} a _ {2}\right).
$$

Multiplying by the transposition $( a _ { 1 } ~ a _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } )$ , we thus see that $U$ contains the transposition $\left( \boldsymbol { a } _ { 1 } ~ \boldsymbol { a } _ { 2 } \right)$ . Conjugating $U$ by an element of ${ \mathfrak { S } } _ { n } \times { \mathfrak { S } } ( n )$ , we may as well suppose that $U$ contains $( n \ n + 1 )$ . But this transposition and ${ \mathfrak { S } } ( n )$ generate $\mathfrak { S } ( n - 1 )$ , and so $U$ contains $\mathfrak { S } ( n - 1 )$ , a contradiction. This proves the claim.

Since $U$ is contained in ${ \mathfrak { S } } _ { n } \times { \mathfrak { S } } ( n )$ and contains ${ \mathfrak { S } } ( n )$ , it necessarily has the form $H \times \mathfrak { S } ( n )$ for some subgroup $H$ of ${ \mathfrak { S } } _ { n }$ , which completes the proof. 

Corollary 14.2. Let $X$ be a transitive $\mathfrak { S }$ -set. Then there exists a map of $\mathfrak { S }$ -sets $X \to \Omega ^ { ( n ) }$ that is everywhere d-to-1, for unique integers $n \geq 0$ and $d \geq 1$ .

15.6. The Levi topology. Recall that $\mathbf { V } _ { n } = \mathbf { F } ^ { n }$ . The standard projection map $\mathbf { V } _ { n + 1 } \to \mathbf { V } _ { n }$ induces an inclusion of dual spaces $\mathbf { V } _ { n } ^ { * } \to \mathbf { V } _ { n + 1 } ^ { * }$ . The restricted dual of $\mathbf { V }$ is $\begin{array} { r } { \mathbf { V } _ { * } = \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } \mathbf { V } _ { n } ^ { * } } \end{array}$ . The group $G$ acts on $\mathbf { V _ { * } }$ , and the action of $G$ on $\mathbf { V } \oplus \mathbf { V } _ { * }$ is oligomorphic. This induces a second pro-oligomorphic topology on $G$ , which we call the Levi topology. The subgroup

$$
L _ {n} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} 1 _ {n} & 0 \\ 0 & * \end{array} \right]
$$

is exactly the subgroup of $G$ fixing each of $e _ { 1 } , \ldots , e _ { n }$ and $e _ { 1 } ^ { * } , \ldots , e _ { n } ^ { * }$ . Thus $L _ { n }$ is open in the Levi topology, and any open subgroup contains some $L _ { n }$ . Write $G ^ { \ell }$ (resp. $G ^ { p }$ ) for the group $G$ equipped with the Levi (resp. parabolic) topology. The ring $\Theta ( G ^ { p } )$ was computed in Theorem 15.7. We now compute $\Theta ( G ^ { \ell } )$ .
Since every open subgroup in the parabolic topology is also open in the Levi topology, there is a continuous homomorphism $G ^ { \ell } \to G ^ { p }$ . This induces a ring homomorphism

$$
\varphi \colon \Theta (G ^ {p}) \to \Theta (G ^ {\ell})
$$
by §3.4(a). The following is our main result on $G ^ { \ell }$ :
Theorem 15.17. The map $\varphi$ is an isomorphism.

We refer to [HS1, §16.6] for the proof. We have not studied the representation categories associated to the group $G ^ { \ell }$ . We expect $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ^ { \ell } ; \mu _ { t } ) = \underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } ( G ^ { p } ; \mu _ { t } )$ for generic $t$ , but that the categories may differ for special values of $t$ . It would be interesting to investigate this in more detail.

15.7. Other linear groups. There are other oligomorphic linear groups, such as the infinite orthogonal, symplectic, and unitary groups. It would be interesting to compute the $\Theta$ rings in these cases. These cases are all smoothly approximable, and so $\Theta \neq 0$ by the results of §6.7. Deligne [Del5] has observed that the infinite orthogonal group admits two 1-parameter families of measures (essentially from approximating it by even or odd finite orthogonal groups), and it seems probable to us that $\Theta \otimes \mathbf { Q }$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf { Q } [ x , y ] / ( x y )$ in this case.

Throughout §16, the word “interval” will mean “open interval in $\mathbf { R }$ .” A left interval is one of the form $( - \infty , a )$ where $a < \infty$ ; right interval is defined analogously. 16.2. Subgroup structure. We begin by classifying the open subgroups of $G$ . For a finite subset $A \subset \mathbf { R }$ , recall that $G ( A )$ is the subgroup of $G$ that fixes each element of $A$ (which, in the present case, is equivalent to fixing the set $A$ ).

Proof. If suffices to show that a subgroup $U$ of $G$ properly containing $G ( A )$ contains some $G ( B )$ with $B$ a proper subset of $A$ . First suppose that $A = \{ x \}$ is a single point, and let $g \in U$ not fix $x$ . Using $g$ and $g ^ { - 1 }$ , we can move $x$ to both a smaller and larger number. Since $G _ { x }$ acts transitively on the intervals $( x , \infty )$ and $( - \infty , x )$ , it follows that for each $a \in \mathbf { R }$ there exists some $g _ { a } \in U$ with $g _ { a } ( x ) = a$ . Now, let $h \in G$ be given. Put $a = h ( x )$ and $h ^ { \prime } = g _ { a } ^ { - 1 } h$ . Then $h ^ { \prime } ( x ) = x$ , and so $h ^ { \prime }$ belongs to $U$ . Since $g _ { a }$ also belongs to $U$ , we find that $h \in U$ , and so $U = G$ , as desired.

Then $G ^ { J } \subset G ( A )$ . Let $h \in G ^ { J }$ not fix $x$ , and put $g ^ { \prime } = g ^ { - 1 } h g$ . Then $g ^ { \prime }$ belongs to $U$ and fixes each $x _ { j }$ for $j \neq i$ . Let $I = ( x _ { i - 1 } , x _ { i + 1 } )$ , with the convention that $x _ { 0 } = - \infty$ and $x _ { n + 1 } = \infty$ . Composing $g ^ { \prime }$ with an element of $G ( A )$ , we can assume that it is the identity outside of $I$ , and thus belongs to $G ^ { I } \subset G$ . By the previous paragraph, $G ^ { I }$ is generated by $G _ { x _ { i } } ^ { I }$ and $g ^ { \prime }$ , and so $U$ contains $G ^ { I }$ . The groups discussed in this section are significant from the perspective of permutation group theory. A permutation group $( \Gamma , \Omega )$ is called highly homogeneous if $\Gamma$ acts transitively on $\Omega ^ { ( n ) }$ for all $n$ . The four groups $G$ , $G ^ { \prime }$ , $H$ , and $H ^ { \prime }$ are all highly homogeneous, as is the infinite symmetric group. Cameron [Cam1] proved that these are the only examples, up to a certain notion of equivalence.

The groups $G$ and $H$ are symmetry groups of one-dimensional manifolds. It would be interesting if one could construct tensor categories associated to higher dimensional manifolds. There is some speculative discussion about this in [HS1, §17.10].

Let $T$ be a boron tree, and let $T _ { H }$ be the set of hydrogen atoms in it. Given $w , x \in T _ { H }$ , there is a unique geodesic in $T$ through $w$ and $x$ . We define a quaternary relation $R$ on $T _ { H }$ by declaring $R ( w , x ; y , z )$ to be true if the geodesic joining $w$ and $x$ meets the one joining $y$ and $z$ . One can show that the tree $T$ can be recovered from the structure $( T _ { H } , R )$ , so the two points of view are equivalent; however, the latter will be more convenient for the moment.

Let $\mathfrak { A }$ be the class of all finite structures on a single quaternary relation that are isomorphic to $( T _ { H } , R )$ for some boron tree $T$ . This is a Fra¨ıss´e class [Cam3, Exercise 2.6.4] (see §6.2 for the definition). Let $\Omega$ be the Fra¨ıss´e limit and let $G$ be its automorphism group. The group $G$ is oligomorphic (with respect to its action on $\Omega$ ).

In §17, we prove two main results: the first (Theorem 17.6) computes $\Theta ( { \mathfrak { A } } )$ ; the second (Theorem 17.10) constructs rigid tensor categories associated to $G$ . We do not completely determine $\Theta ( G )$ , but one could by extending our methods. The discussion in this section illustrates how measures can be effectively studied from the model-theoretic perspective developed in §6.

Lemma 17.9. We have $c \cdot ( 2 c + 1 ) = 0$ .
Proof. Regard $\mathbf { T } _ { 3 }$ as the subtree of $\mathbf { T } _ { 5 }$ obtained by deleting $p$ and $q$ . We thus have

$$
\left[ \mathbf {T} _ {3} \subset \mathbf {T} _ {5} \right] = \left[ \mathbf {T} _ {3} \subset \mathbf {T} _ {5} ^ {p} \right] \cdot \left[ \mathbf {T} _ {5} ^ {p} \subset \mathbf {T} _ {5} \right] = \left[ \mathbf {T} _ {3} \subset \mathbf {T} _ {5} ^ {q} \right] \cdot \left[ \mathbf {T} _ {5} ^ {q} \subset \mathbf {T} _ {5} \right].
$$

Note that $[ \mathbf { T } _ { 3 } \subset \mathbf { T } _ { 5 } ^ { p } ] = [ \mathbf { T } _ { 3 } \subset \mathbf { T } _ { 5 } ^ { q } ] = \alpha _ { 4 }$ since $\mathbf { T } _ { 5 } ^ { p }$ and $\mathbf { T } _ { 5 } ^ { q }$ are just copies of $\mathbf { T } _ { 4 }$ . Thus the above equation yields

$$

Using the formulas for these quantities in terms of $c$ from the previous lemma yields the result. 

Proof of Theorem 17.6. Let $R = \mathbf { Z } [ x ] / ( x ( 2 x + 1 ) )$ . The above lemmas show that we have a surjective ring homomorphism $i \colon R \to \Theta ( { \mathfrak { A } } )$ given by $i ( x ) = c$ . Now, $R$ is $\mathbf { Z }$ -torsion free and $R \otimes \mathbf { Q }$ is isomorphic (as a ring) to $\mathbf Q \times \mathbf Q$ . The existence of the measures $\mu , \nu \colon \Theta ( \mathfrak { A } ) \to \mathbf { Q }$ thus shows that $i$ is injective. (Note that $\mu ( c ) = - \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } }$ and $\nu ( c ) = 0$ .) Thus $i$ is an isomorphism.

We now turn to $\Theta ^ { * } ( { \mathfrak { A } } )$ . By the above, we have an isomorphism $R [ 1 / x ]  \Theta ( \mathfrak { A } ) [ 1 / c ]$ , and clearly $R [ 1 / x ] \cong \mathbf { Z } [ 1 / 2 ]$ . If $i$ is an embedding in $\mathfrak { A }$ then $[ i ] = \pm 3 / 2 ^ { n }$ in $\Theta ( \mathfrak { A } ) [ 1 / c ] \cong \mathbf { Z } [ 1 / 2 ]$ . Inverting these classes, we find $\Theta ^ { * } ( \mathfrak { A } ) = \mathbf { Z } [ 1 / 6 ]$ , as claimed. 

17.4. Representation categories. Recall that $\Omega$ is the Fra¨ıss´e limit of the class $\mathfrak { A }$ , and $G$ is its automorphism group. For a finite subset $A$ of $\Omega$ recall that $G ( A )$ is the subgroup of $G$ fixing each element of $A$ . We let $\mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { O } }$ be the collection of all subgroups of the form $G ( A )$ . This is the stabilizer class generated by $\Omega$ . By Theorem 6.9, we have $\Theta ^ { * } ( \mathfrak { V } ) = \Theta ^ { * } ( G ; \mathcal { E } )$ . We let $\mu _ { 1 }$ be the $\mathbf { Z } [ 1 / 6 ]$ -valued measure for $( G , \mathcal { E } )$ corresponding to $\mu$ under this isomorphism. Fix a field $k$ of characteristic $\neq 2 , 3$ ; we also regard $\mu _ { 1 }$ as $k$ -valued in what follows. The following is our main result on tensor categories coming from boron trees:
Theorem 17.10. The Karoubi envelope of $\underline { { \mathrm { P e r m } } } _ { k } ( G , \mathcal { E } ; \mu _ { 1 } )$ is a semi-simple pre-Tannakian category.
We require some lemmas before proving the theorem.
Lemma 17.11. Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are finite subsets of $\Omega$ such that $G ( B )$ is contained in $G ( A )$ with finite index. Then $A = B$ .

Proof. Replacing $B$ with $A \cup B$ , we can assume that $A \subset B$ . Suppose that this containment is proper and that $G ( B )$ has finite index in $G ( A )$ ; we will produce a contradiction. Recall that $\Omega ^ { [ A ] }$ denotes the set of embeddings $A  \Omega$ , and this is isomorphic to $G / G ( A )$ . Since $G ( B )$ has finite index in $G ( A )$ , the fibers of $\Omega ^ { [ B ] } \to \Omega ^ { [ A ] }$ have finite cardinality, say $n$ . This means that the standard embedding $A  \Omega$ can be extended in only $n$ ways to $B$ . However, it is easy to write down a finite boron tree $C$ and an embedding $A  C$ that extends to $B$ in $> n$ ways. Since $C$ embeds into $\Omega$ , this gives a contradiction. 

For a finite subset $A$ of $\Omega$ , let $G \vert A \vert$ be the subgroup fixing $A$ as a set. By the above lemma, $G [ A ]$ is exactly the normalizer in $G$ of $G ( A )$ . We let $\mathcal { E } ^ { + }$ be the set of all subgroups $U$ of $G$ such that $G ( A ) \subset U \subset G [ A ]$ for some $A$ ; it is easily seen to be a stabilizer class.
Lemma 17.12. We have the following:

(b) If $X$ is an $\mathcal { E } ^ { + }$ -smooth $G$ -set and $H$ is a subgroup of $\operatorname { A u t } ( X )$ then $X / H$ is $\mathcal { E } ^ { + }$ -smooth.
(c) If $X$ is an $\mathcal { E } ^ { + }$ -smooth set then so is $X ^ { ( n ) }$ for any $n \geq 0$

The intersection of all conjugates of $G ( A )$ in $U$ has the form $G ( B )$ , and is contained in $G ( A )$ with finite index, and is thus equal to $G ( A )$ by Lemma 17.11. Thus $G ( A )$ is normal in $U$ and so $U$ is contained in the normalizer of $G ( A )$ , which is $G \vert A \vert$ . Thus $U \in \mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { + } }$ , as required.

Write $X = G / U$ where $U \in \mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { + } }$ Then $\operatorname { A u t } ( X ) = \operatorname { N } ( U ) / U$ , and so $H$ corresponds to a subgroup $V$ between $U$ and $\mathrm { N } ( U )$ Since $H$ is finite (Proposition 2.8(d)), $V$ contains $U$ with finite index, and so $V \in \mathcal { E } ^ { + }$ by (a). We have $X / H = G / V$ , and so $X / H$ is $\mathcal { E } ^ { + }$ -smooth.

Lemma 17.13. Let $T$ be a boron tree. Then $\mathrm { A u t } ( T )$ has order $2 ^ { r } 3 ^ { s }$ with $s \in \{ 0 , 1 \}$

Proof. If $\# T \leq 3$ this is clear. Suppose now that $\# T \geq 4$ . Let $T ^ { \prime }$ be the boron tree obtained from $T$ by deleting all paired vertices, and converting the neighboring boron atoms to hydrogen. Any automorphism of $T$ restricts to an automorphism of $T ^ { \prime }$ , and we have an exact sequence

$$
1 \to (\mathbf {Z} / 2 \mathbf {Z}) ^ {r} \to \mathrm {A u t} (T) \to \mathrm {A u t} (T ^ {\prime})
$$

where $r$ is the number of pairs of paired vertices in $T$ . (The $\mathbf { Z } / 2 \mathbf { Z }$ factors here are involutions that swap paired vertices.) The result is true for $T ^ { \prime }$ by induction, and thus for $T$ by the above sequence. 

Every member of $\mathcal { E } ^ { + }$ contains a member of $\mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { O } }$ with finite index, and so $\mathcal { E } ^ { \sigma }$ is “large” in $\mathcal { E } ^ { + }$ in (a relative analog of) the sense of §3.4(d). Thus $\Theta ^ { * } ( G ; \mathcal { E } ^ { + } ) \otimes \mathbf { Q } = \Theta ^ { * } ( G ; \mathcal { E } ) \otimes \mathbf { Q }$ , and so $\mu _ { 1 }$ extends uniquely to a homomorphism $\mu _ { 2 } \colon \Theta ^ { * } ( G ; \mathcal { E } ^ { + } ) \to \mathbf { Q }$ .
Lemma 17.14. $\mu _ { 2 }$ takes values in $\mathbf { Z } [ 1 / 6 ]$ , and is regular if regarded as a $\mathbf { Z } [ 1 / 6 ]$ -valued measure for $( G , \mathcal { E } ^ { + } )$ .
Proof. Let $U \in \mathcal { E } ^ { \mathcal { + } }$ , and let $A$ be a finite subset of $\Omega$ such that $G ( A ) \subset U \subset G [ A ]$ . Then

We know that the numerator has the form $\pm 2 ^ { - r } 3 ^ { s }$ . The denominator divides $[ G [ A ] : G ( A ) ]$ , which has the form $2 ^ { r } 3 ^ { s }$ by Lemma 17.13. (We note that $G [ A ] / G ( A )$ is the automorphism group of the boron tree structure on $A$ induced from that on $\Omega$ .) Thus the result follows. 

Proof of Theorem 17.10. Regard $\mu _ { 2 }$ as a $k$ -valued measure. Since it takes values in the (image of) $\mathbf { Z } [ 1 / 6 ]$ , it satisfies condition (P) from Definition 7.10. By Lemma 17.12(c), $\mathcal { E } ^ { + }$ satisfies condition (∗) from Remark 5.7. By Theorem 13.2 in the relative case (see §13.4), the category $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } _ { k } ( G , { \mathcal { E } } ^ { + } ; \mu _ { 2 } )$ is semi-simple and locally pre-Tannakian. The functor

$$
\underline {{\mathrm {P e r m}}} _ {k} (G, \mathcal {E}; \mu_ {1}) \to \underline {{\mathrm {R e p}}} _ {k} (G, \mathcal {E} ^ {+}; \mu_ {2})
$$

is fully faithful, and every object in the target is a quotient of something in the image. Since the target category is semi-simple, it is therefore equivalent to the Karoubi envelope of the source. This completes the proof. 

Remark 17.15. Theorem 17.10 implies that $\mu _ { 1 }$ extends to a regular measure for $G$ . This follows from the main results of [HS4]. See [HS1, §18] for a proof of the weaker result that $\mu _ { 1 }$ extends to a normal measure for $G$ . 

Remark 17.16. Arguing as in §16.7, one can show that $\underline { { \mathrm { R e p } } } _ { k } ^ { \mathrm { f } } ( G ; \mu ^ { \prime } )$ cannot be obtained by interpolating finite groups: again, $G$ acts transitively on $\Omega ^ { ( 5 ) }$ and not $\Omega ^ { [ 5 ] }$ . (In this case, one could also use the fact that $G$ is 3-transitive and appeal to the classification of 3-transitive finite groups [Cam4, Theorem 5.2].) 

Remark 17.17. With Nekrasov, we investigate tree categories further in [HNS]. For every $d \geq 3$ , there are analogs of $\mu$ and $\nu$ for trees of valence at most $d$ , as well as two one-parameter families of measures on unbounded valence trees which “interpolate” these. 
